components.note: 田 (field/land) reflects that 畿 names territory — specifically the land immediately surrounding a capital.

戈 (gē) is marked as the phonetic element here, but gē does not closely resemble jī. The real historical phonetic in 畿 is 幾 (jī) — 戈 is only a fragment of that fuller character captured by this partial decomposition.

example.hanzi: 西安曾经是中国古代的京畿。
example.pinyin: Xī’ān céngjīng shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de jīngjī.
example.english: Xi’an was once the capital region of ancient China.
example.fact: 畿 appears almost exclusively in 京畿 (jīngjī), "the area surrounding the capital" — a term used throughout imperial Chinese history for the region administered directly around the emperor’s seat.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows that dusting is an action done by hand.
单 (dān) is close to dǎn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 妈妈用掸子掸去桌上的灰尘。
example.pinyin: Māma yòng dǎnzi dǎnqù zhuō shàng de huīchén.
example.english: Mom used a duster to dust the dirt off the table.
example.fact: 掸 is also used to write 掸族 (Dǎnzú), the Chinese name for the Shan people of Myanmar.

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks that fetters are made of metal.
尞 (liáo) is close to liào’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 犯人的脚上戴着铁镣。
example.pinyin: Fànrén de jiǎo shàng dàizhe tiěliào.
example.english: The prisoner wears iron shackles on his feet.
example.fact: 镣 almost always appears paired with another character, as in 脚镣 (jiǎoliào, "leg irons") or 镣铐 (liàokào, "shackles and handcuffs") — the latter sharing the same 钅 metal radical.

components.note: 马 (horse) marks the character as horse-related — an excellent, spirited horse.
尧 (yáo) belongs to the same phonetic series as 骁, but the modern reading has diverged (x- vs y-); the connection is historical rather than audible today.

example.hanzi: 他骑着一匹骁勇的战马。
example.pinyin: Tā qízhe yī pǐ xiāoyǒng de zhànmǎ.
example.english: He rode a brave, valiant war horse.
example.fact: 骁 appears almost exclusively in 骁勇 (xiāoyǒng, "brave and valiant"), traditionally used in classical texts to describe fierce warriors and their horses.

components.note: 木 (wood) marks that rafters and beams are made of wood.
彖 (tuàn) shares the final -uan with chuán, though the initial consonant has shifted over the centuries — only a loose match remains.

example.hanzi: 老房子的椽子已经腐烂了。
example.pinyin: Lǎo fángzi de chuánzi yǐjīng fǔlàn le.
example.english: The old house’s rafters have already rotted.
example.fact: 椽 appears in the idiom 大笔如椽 ("a writing brush as big as a roof beam"), which describes especially powerful, influential writing — from a Jin-dynasty story of an official who dreamed of receiving a rafter-sized brush before drafting an important state document.

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 侗 as describing a person’s character or a group of people.
同 (tóng) is close to dòng’s reading — same final and a related initial, differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 侗族主要生活在中国南方。
example.pinyin: Dòngzú zhǔyào shēnghuó zài Zhōngguó nánfāng.
example.english: The Dong people mainly live in southern China.
example.fact: 侗 is best known today as the name of the Dong ethnic minority (侗族), known for their distinctive wooden drum towers and covered "wind-and-rain" bridges.

meanings: river and county in Hebei province

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 滦 as a river name.
栾 (luán) gives the sound — an exact match with 滦’s reading.

example.hanzi: 滦河从河北流过，最后注入渤海。
example.pinyin: Luánhé cóng Héběi liúguò, zuìhòu zhùrù Bóhǎi.
example.english: The Luan River flows through Hebei and finally empties into the Bohai Sea.
example.fact: 滦 names the Luan River (滦河) in Hebei province, which flows into the Bohai Sea near the coastal city of Qinhuangdao.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 荩 as originally naming a kind of grass/weed.
尽 (jìn) gives the sound — an exact match with 荩’s reading.

example.hanzi: 古人称赞忠诚正直的臣子为荩臣。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén chēngzàn zhōngchéng zhèngzhí de chénzǐ wéi jìnchén.
example.english: People in ancient times praised loyal, upright officials as "jinchen".
example.fact: 荩 appears in the literary compound 荩臣 (jìnchén, "loyal minister"), where the sense of "faithfulness" extends metaphorically from a plant name to loyalty in classical political writing.

meanings: classifier for a body of clear water
etymologyHint: Expansive 弘 water 氵; 弘 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 泓 as describing a body of water.
弘 (hóng) is pronounced identically to 泓’s reading.

example.hanzi: 院子里有一泓清泉。
example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ yǒu yī hóng qīngquán.
example.english: There is a pool of clear spring water in the courtyard.
example.fact: 泓 doubles as a measure word (classifier) for a body of still, clear water, as in 一泓清泉 — one of the more unusual and poetic classifiers in Chinese.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蚱 as an insect.
乍 (zhà) gives the sound — an exact match with 蚱’s reading.

example.hanzi: 蚱蜢在草地上跳来跳去。
example.pinyin: Zhàměng zài cǎodì shàng tiào lái tiào qù.
example.english: Grasshoppers hop around on the grass.
example.fact: 蚱 almost never appears alone in modern Chinese — it survives only in 蚱蜢 (zhàměng, "grasshopper").

components.note: 疒 (sickness) marks 癜 as a medical term for a skin condition.
殿 (diàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 癜’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他脸上长了白癜风。
example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng zhǎngle báidiànfēng.
example.english: He developed vitiligo on his face.
example.fact: 癜 appears in 白癜风 (báidiànfēng), the Chinese medical term for vitiligo, a condition that causes patches of skin to lose their pigment.

components.note: 酉 (wine vessel) is used as the chemistry radical for many organic-compound characters, including 酯.
旨 (zhǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 酯’s reading.

example.hanzi: 甘油三酯会影响心血管健康。
example.pinyin: Gānyóusānzhǐ huì yǐngxiǎng xīnxuèguǎn jiànkāng.
example.english: Triglycerides can affect cardiovascular health.
example.fact: 酯 is the standard character for "ester" in chemistry; 甘油三酯 (gānyóusānzhǐ, "triglycerides") is a term that appears on routine Chinese blood-test reports.

components.note: 骨 (bone) marks 體 as relating to the physical body.
豊 is read lǐ in modern dictionaries, which has diverged sharply from tǐ — the sound link reflects a much earlier stage of the language.

example.hanzi: 他的身體很健康。
example.pinyin: Tā de shēntǐ hěn jiànkāng.
example.english: His body is very healthy.
example.fact: 體 is the traditional, unsimplified form of 体 — one of the most common characters in Chinese. Simplification replaced 體’s complex 骨+豊 structure with the far simpler 亻+本, cutting the stroke count from 22 down to just 7.

example.hanzi: 癸是十天干中的最后一个。
example.pinyin: Guǐ shì shí tiāngān zhōng de zuìhòu yī gè.
example.english: Gui is the last of the Ten Heavenly Stems.
example.fact: The Ten Heavenly Stems (天干: 甲乙丙丁戊己庚辛壬癸) combine with the Twelve Earthly Branches to form the 60-term sexagenary cycle traditionally used in China to count years, days, and hours — a system still used today for naming years.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蚜 as an insect.
牙 (yá) gives the sound — an exact match with 蚜’s reading.

example.hanzi: 蚜虫会吃掉植物的叶子。
example.pinyin: Yáchóng huì chīdiào zhíwù de yèzi.
example.english: Aphids eat away at plants’ leaves.
example.fact: Ladybugs (瓢虫) are natural predators of aphids (蚜虫) and are deliberately released in organic farming as a pesticide-free way to control them.

components.note: 扌 (hand) marks 扪 as an action done with the hand.
门 (mén) gives the sound — an exact match with 扪’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他扪心自问，觉得很惭愧。
example.pinyin: Tā ménxīn zìwèn, juéde hěn cánkuì.
example.english: He asked himself honestly and felt very ashamed.
example.fact: 扪 survives today mainly in the idiom 扪心自问 (ménxīn zìwèn, literally "touch the heart and ask oneself"), meaning "to search one’s conscience" — otherwise it is nearly obsolete in modern speech.

components.note: 广 (shelter) marks 庑 as relating to a building or structure.
无 (wú) is close to wǔ’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古代宫殿两侧有长长的廊庑。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài gōngdiàn liǎng cè yǒu chángcháng de lángwǔ.
example.english: Ancient palaces had long corridors running along both sides.
example.fact: 庑 appears in 廊庑 (lángwǔ), the covered walkways bordering the courtyards of traditional Chinese palace and temple architecture — still visible today in Beijing’s Forbidden City.

components.note: 欠 (to owe/yawn) contributes an abstract sense tied to desire and breath.
音 (yīn) shares the final -in and tone with xīn, though the initial consonant differs — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 古人认为祖先会歆享祭品。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén rènwéi zǔxiān huì xīnxiǎng jìpǐn.
example.english: Ancient people believed ancestors would happily accept the sacrificial offerings.
example.fact: 歆 described how spirits or ancestors were believed to "enjoy" (歆享, xīnxiǎng) the aroma of sacrificial offerings in ancient Chinese ritual — reflecting how early religious practice linked scent to spiritual nourishment.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蝮 as a creature classified with insects and reptiles.
复 (fù) gives the sound — an exact match with 蝮’s reading.

example.hanzi: 蝮蛇的毒性很强。
example.pinyin: Fùshé de dúxìng hěn qiáng.
example.english: The pit viper’s venom is very potent.
example.fact: 蝮蛇 (fùshé) refers to pit vipers of the genus Gloydius found across China, identifiable by the heat-sensing pit between the eye and nostril.

components.note: 足 (foot) marks 蹶 as relating to the feet or legs — stumbling, falling.
厥 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 蹶’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他一不小心蹶了一下，差点摔倒。
example.pinyin: Tā yī bù xiǎoxīn juéle yīxià, chàdiǎn shuāidǎo.
example.english: He stumbled carelessly for a moment and nearly fell.
example.fact: 蹶 appears in the idiom 一蹶不振 (yī jué bù zhèn, "to stumble once and never rise again"), describing someone who suffers a single setback so severe they never recover.

meanings: ancient name for go (Chinese board game)

components.note: 廾 (two hands) suggests the manual handling of game pieces.
亦 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 弈’s reading.

example.hanzi: 两位棋手正在对弈。
example.pinyin: Liǎng wèi qíshǒu zhèngzài duìyì.
example.english: Two chess players are playing against each other.
example.fact: 弈 specifically denoted the game of Go (Weiqi) in classical usage; 对弈 (duìyì, "to play against each other") remains the standard formal term for a Go match today.

meanings: a cupboard or pantry to store
(literary) to store; to keep; to preserve

components.note: 广 (shelter) marks 庋 as relating to a structure for storage.
支 (zhī) has diverged substantially in sound from guǐ — only a distant historical connection remains, no longer transparent in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 他把书都庋藏在阁楼里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shū dōu guǐcáng zài gélóu lǐ.
example.english: He stored all his books away in the attic.
example.fact: 庋 is a literary word for shelving or putting things away for safekeeping; it survives mainly in the bookish compound 庋藏 (guǐcáng, "to store away"), used in writing about archives and collections.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 喟 as relating to a sound made with the mouth — a sigh.
胃 (wèi) has diverged sharply in its initial sound from kuì — only a loose historical connection remains.

example.hanzi: 他喟然长叹一声。
example.pinyin: Tā kuìrán cháng tàn yī shēng.
example.english: He let out a long sigh.
example.fact: 喟 typically appears in the literary phrase 喟然 (kuìrán, "sighingly") or 喟叹 (kuìtàn, "to sigh") — both belong to formal, written Chinese rather than everyday speech.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 滂 as describing rushing water or heavy rain.
旁 (páng) is close to pāng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 外面下着滂沱大雨。
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn xiàzhe pāngtuó dàyǔ.
example.english: Outside it is pouring down torrential rain.
example.fact: 滂 appears almost exclusively in 滂沱 (pāngtuó), describing torrential, pouring rain — one of the most common ways to intensify "heavy rain" in written Chinese.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 啕 as relating to a sound made with the mouth — wailing.
匋 (táo) gives the sound — an exact match with 啕’s reading.

example.hanzi: 孩子哭得号啕不已。
example.pinyin: Háizi kūde háotáo bùyǐ.
example.english: The child cried and wailed without stopping.
example.fact: 啕 exists almost solely in 号啕 or 嚎啕 (háotáo, "to wail loudly"), most often seen in the set phrase 号啕大哭 for uncontrollable crying.

components.note: 虫 (bug) is used broadly in Chinese for small creatures, including shellfish like the oyster.
厉 (lì) gives the sound — an exact match with 蛎’s reading.

example.hanzi: 生蚝也叫牡蛎，很多人喜欢吃。
example.pinyin: Shēngháo yě jiào mǔlì, hěn duō rén xǐhuan chī.
example.english: Oysters, also called "muli", are enjoyed by many people.
example.fact: 蛎 appears in 牡蛎 (mǔlì), the standard Chinese word for "oyster" — one of the most widely farmed shellfish along China’s coast, especially in Fujian and Shandong.

components.note: 犭 (animal) marks 獭 as a mammal.
赖 (lài) has diverged substantially in sound from tǎ — initial, vowel, and tone all differ, leaving only a loose historical link.

example.hanzi: 水獭生活在河流和湖泊里。
example.pinyin: Shuǐtǎ shēnghuó zài héliú hé húbó lǐ.
example.english: Otters live in rivers and lakes.
example.fact: 水獭 (shuǐtǎ, "otter") are skilled swimmers with webbed feet and dense waterproof fur, and in China they are a protected species after historical overhunting for their pelts.

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 槁 as relating to plants and trees — withering.
高 (gāo) is close to gǎo’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 秋天里，树叶渐渐枯槁。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān lǐ, shùyè jiànjiàn kūgǎo.
example.english: In autumn, the leaves gradually wither.
example.fact: 槁 pairs with 枯 in 枯槁 (kūgǎo), a literary compound describing withered plants or, metaphorically, a gaunt, lifeless human appearance — common in classical poetry about hardship.

components.note: 羽 (feather) marks 翊 as relating to flight, and by extension, assistance (as if lending wings).
立 (lì) has diverged from yì in its initial sound — only the tone matches, leaving a loose connection.

example.hanzi: "翊"这个字常用在人名里。
example.pinyin: "Yì" zhège zì cháng yòng zài rénmíng lǐ.
example.english: The character "yi" is often used in given names.
example.fact: 翊 originally meant "to assist" (as in the ancient official title 翊卫, "imperial guard"), and today survives mainly as a literary character chosen for personal names for its associations with support and flight.

meanings: used in 齷齪|龌龊[wo4 chuo4]

components.note: 足 (foot) is the semantic component here per the source data, though the connection to "narrow, dirty" is not obvious — the two characters of 龌龊 may simply share components for visual/structural reasons.
齿 (chǐ) shares only the initial ch- with chuò; the vowel and tone differ, so the sound match is loose.

example.hanzi: 他觉得这种龌龊的手段很可耻。
example.pinyin: Tā juéde zhè zhǒng wòchuò de shǒuduàn hěn kěchǐ.
example.english: He felt that such dirty, underhanded methods were shameful.
example.fact: 龌龊 (wòchuò) originally described something physically cramped and filthy, but in modern Chinese it is used almost entirely figuratively, for morally low or underhanded behavior.

components.note: 阝 (place/mound) marks 邺 as a place name.
业 (yè) gives the sound — an exact match with 邺’s reading.

example.hanzi: 邺城曾是三国时期曹操的都城。
example.pinyin: Yèchéng céng shì Sānguó shíqí Cáo Cāo de dūchéng.
example.english: Ye City was once the capital of Cao Cao during the Three Kingdoms period.
example.fact: 邺 (Ye) was the capital of Cao Cao’s Wei state during the Three Kingdoms period and later served as a capital for several other dynasties — its ruins lie near modern Handan, on the Hebei-Henan border.

meanings: a marsh plant whose root is used for medicine

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 莘 as originally naming a marsh plant.
辛 (xīn) has diverged from shēn in its initial sound — only the tone matches.

example.hanzi: 莘莘学子怀着梦想走进校园。
example.pinyin: Shēnshēn xuézǐ huáizhe mèngxiǎng zǒujìn xiàoyuán.
example.english: Throngs of students walk onto campus carrying their dreams.
example.fact: 莘 survives mainly in the literary phrase 莘莘学子 (shēnshēn xuézǐ, "a great multitude of students"), often used in graduation speeches and news articles, where 莘莘 simply means "numerous".

example.hanzi: 古人认为宰相要能燮理阴阳。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén rènwéi zǎixiàng yào néng xièlǐ yīnyáng.
example.english: Ancient people believed a chief minister should be able to "harmonize yin and yang".
example.fact: 燮 appears in the classical phrase 燮理阴阳, historically describing a top minister’s duty to govern so skillfully that heaven and earth stayed in balance — reflecting how ancient Chinese political philosophy linked good governance to cosmic harmony.

components.note: 刂 (knife) marks 剁 as a cutting action.
朵 (duǒ) is close to duò’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她正在厨房里剁肉。
example.pinyin: Tā zhèngzài chúfáng lǐ duò ròu.
example.english: She is chopping meat in the kitchen.
example.fact: 剁 describes a chopping motion straight down, as with a cleaver mincing meat — distinct from 切 (qiē), which describes a slicing motion. Chinese has many such precise verbs for different cutting techniques.

meanings: (history) to have an audience with the Emperor

components.note: 见 (to see) marks 觐 as relating to an audience — seeing someone of high status.
堇 (jǐn) is close to jìn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 大臣进京觐见皇帝。
example.pinyin: Dàchén jìn jīng jìnjiàn huángdì.
example.english: The minister went to the capital to have an audience with the emperor.
example.fact: 觐 survives mainly in 觐见 (jìnjiàn), the formal historical term for a subject’s audience with an emperor, and in modern diplomatic language, for a head of state’s formal visit to a monarch.

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 铛 as a metal object.
当 (dāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 铛’s reading in this onomatopoeic sense.

example.hanzi: 硬币掉在地上，发出叮当的声音。
example.pinyin: Yìngbì diào zài dìshàng, fāchū dīngdāng de shēngyīn.
example.english: The coin fell on the ground, making a clinking sound.
example.fact: 铛 is polyphonic: read dāng it is an onomatopoeia for a clinking or clanging metallic sound (叮当, dīngdāng), while read chēng it names a flat metal pan or griddle (饼铛, "pancake griddle") — the meaning depends entirely on which reading is used.

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 谗 as relating to spoken words — slander.

免 (miǎn) is listed as the phonetic element here, but on its own it does not sound like chán. It is a fragment of the fuller historical phonetic 毚 (chán, "cunning rabbit"), which this partial decomposition only captured part of.

example.hanzi: 他因为听信谗言而冤枉了忠臣。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi tīngxìn chányán ér yuānwang le zhōngchén.
example.english: He wronged a loyal minister because he believed slanderous words.
example.fact: 谗言 (chányán, "slanderous words") is a recurring theme in classical Chinese historical writing, where honest officials were often undone by rivals whispering chányán into the ruler’s ear.

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 镍 as a metal.
臬 (niè) gives the sound — an exact match with 镍’s reading.

example.hanzi: 硬币里含有镍。
example.pinyin: Yìngbì lǐ hányǒu niè.
example.english: Coins contain nickel.
example.fact: Chemical elements that are metals almost always use the 钅 radical in Chinese, combined with a phonetic borrowing — the same pattern used for 钙 (calcium), 钾 (potassium), and 镉 (cadmium).

meanings: used in 臃腫|臃肿[yong1 zhong3]

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks 臃 as relating to the body — swelling.
雍 (yōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 臃’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他因为穿得太厚而显得臃肿。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi chuān de tài hòu ér xiǎnde yōngzhǒng.
example.english: He looked bulky because he was dressed too thickly.
example.fact: 臃 appears almost exclusively in 臃肿 (yōngzhǒng), meaning "bloated" or "overly bulky" — used both literally for swollen body parts and figuratively for an inefficient, overstaffed organization.

components.note: 土 (earth) marks 墒 as relating to soil.
商 (shāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 墒’s reading.

example.hanzi: 春雨过后，田里的墒情很好。
example.pinyin: Chūnyǔ guòhòu, tián lǐ de shāngqíng hěn hǎo.
example.english: After the spring rain, the soil moisture in the fields is good.
example.fact: 墒情 (shāngqíng, "soil moisture condition") is a standard term in Chinese agricultural weather reports, used by farmers and meteorologists to judge whether fields are ready for planting.

etymologyHint: A flower 华 blooming in the sun 日

components.note: 日 (sun) contributes the image of sunlight.
华 (flower/splendor) combines with 日 to form the idea of radiant brightness — sunlight on a blooming flower.

example.hanzi: "晔"是一个常用于人名的字，寓意光明兴盛。
example.pinyin: "Yè" shì yī gè chángyòng yú rénmíng de zì, yùyì guāngmíng xīngshèng.
example.english: "Ye" is a character commonly used in given names, symbolizing brightness and prosperity.
example.fact: 晔 was the given name of Emperor Zhaozong of Tang (唐昭宗), Li Ye (李晔), one of the last emperors of the Tang dynasty, who reigned during its final decline in the early 10th century.

etymologyHint: To roast 火 meat on a spit 番; 番 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) marks 燔 as a burning action.
番 (fān) is close to fán’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古人会燔烧祭品来祭天。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén huì fánshāo jìpǐn lái jì tiān.
example.english: Ancient people would burn sacrificial offerings to worship heaven.
example.fact: 燔 specifically referred to burning sacrificial offerings (as in 燔祭, "burnt offering") in ancient Chinese ritual — a ceremonial use of fire distinct from ordinary cooking or destruction.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 嘭 as a sound.
彭 (péng) is close to pēng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 气球突然"嘭"的一声破了。
example.pinyin: Qìqiú tūrán "pēng" de yī shēng pòle.
example.english: The balloon suddenly burst with a "peng" sound.
example.fact: 嘭 is a purely onomatopoeic character for a dull thump or pop, like a balloon bursting — sound-effect characters in Chinese almost always carry the 口 ("mouth") radical.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 涿 as relating to dripping water.
豖 has diverged substantially in sound from zhuō, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 涿州是河北省的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzhōu shì Héběi Shěng de yī gè chéngshì.
example.english: Zhuozhou is a city in Hebei province.
example.fact: 涿 survives today mainly in the place name 涿州 (Zhuōzhōu), a city in Hebei near Beijing traditionally said to be the hometown of the Han-dynasty hero Liu Bei from Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

components.note: 酉 (wine vessel) marks 醯 as relating to fermented liquids — vinegar.
㐬 is a rare component whose historical pronunciation is uncertain; the phonetic connection to xī is not clearly established.

example.hanzi: 古代常用"醯"字表示醋。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài chángyòng "xī" zì biǎoshì cù.
example.english: In ancient times, the character "xi" was often used to mean vinegar.
example.fact: 醯 is the classical Chinese word for vinegar, largely replaced by 醋 (cù) in modern usage — it survives mainly in classical texts and discussions of historical Chinese cooking and chemistry terminology.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) marks 箩 as a bamboo object — a basket.
罗 (luó) gives the sound — an exact match with 箩’s reading.

example.hanzi: 农民用箩筐装满了谷子。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng luókuāng zhuāngmǎnle gǔzi.
example.english: The farmer filled the bamboo baskets with grain.
example.fact: 箩筐 (luókuāng) are traditional woven bamboo baskets long used across rural China for carrying and storing harvested grain and vegetables.

components.note: 阝 (place/mound) marks 鄱 as a place name.
番 has readings fān and pān, neither of which closely matches pó — the sound has diverged substantially in this place name.

example.hanzi: 鄱阳湖是中国最大的淡水湖。
example.pinyin: Póyáng Hú shì Zhōngguó zuìdà de dànshuǐhú.
example.english: Poyang Lake is China’s largest freshwater lake.
example.fact: 鄱阳湖 (Poyang Lake) in Jiangxi province is China’s largest freshwater lake, acting as a seasonal flood buffer for the Yangtze River and a major wintering site for migratory birds, including the rare Siberian crane.

components.note: 目 (eye) marks 睨 as relating to looking.
兒 (ní) is close to nì’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他斜睨了一眼那个人。
example.pinyin: Tā xiénì le yīyǎn nàge rén.
example.english: He glanced sideways scornfully at that person.
example.fact: 睨 typically pairs with 斜 in 斜睨 (xiénì), describing a scornful sidelong glance — a literary word choice favored in fiction over the plain verb 看 ("to look").

meanings: to warn sb of their errors
etymologyHint: Fighting 争 words 讠; 争 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 诤 as relating to spoken words — arguing or remonstrating.
争 (zhēng) is pronounced identically to 诤’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他敢于向国君直言诤谏。
example.pinyin: Tā gǎnyú xiàng guójūn zhíyán zhēngjiàn.
example.english: He dared to speak frankly and remonstrate with the ruler.
example.fact: 诤 carries the meaning "to remonstrate" — historically, a minister willing to offer blunt criticism to the ruler was considered essential to good government in Confucian political thought, in contrast to sycophantic courtiers.

components.note: 土 (earth) marks 坳 as relating to the ground — a hollow or depression.
幼 (yòu) has diverged substantially in sound from ào, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 山坳里有一个小村庄。
example.pinyin: Shān’ào lǐ yǒu yī gè xiǎo cūnzhuāng.
example.english: There is a small village in the mountain hollow.
example.fact: 坳 appears in 山坳 (shān’ào), a common term in Chinese landscape description for a low, sheltered dip between hills — often the site of small villages seeking shelter from the wind.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) marks 鹭 as a bird.
路 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 鹭’s reading.

example.hanzi: 白鹭在河边悠闲地散步。
example.pinyin: Báilù zài hébiān yōuxián de sànbù.
example.english: The white egret strolls leisurely by the riverside.
example.fact: 白鹭 (báilù, "little egret") is a common wading bird across East Asia and a frequent subject in classical Chinese poetry, symbolizing purity and tranquility because of its white plumage.

components.note: 石 (stone) is used as a mineral-related radical for 砷.
申 (shēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 砷’s reading.

example.hanzi: 砷是一种有毒的化学元素。
example.pinyin: Shēn shì yī zhǒng yǒudú de huàxué yuánsù.
example.english: Arsenic is a toxic chemical element.
example.fact: Arsenic (砷) is best known as a historical poison, but in carefully controlled medicinal doses it is also the active compound in arsenic trioxide, a treatment studied and used for certain forms of leukemia.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 唏 as a sound made with the mouth — sobbing.
希 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 唏’s reading.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息，她不禁唏嘘。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā bùjīn xīxū.
example.english: Hearing this news, she could not help but sigh with sorrow.
example.fact: 唏 appears in 唏嘘 (xīxū), a word describing a mix of sighing and sniffling in response to sad or moving news — commonly used in modern Chinese to express sympathy or nostalgia.

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 伲 as a pronoun referring to people.
尼 (ní) is close to nì’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 上海话里，"伲"有时用来表示"我们"。
example.pinyin: Shànghǎi huà lǐ, "nì" yǒushí yòng lái biǎoshì "wǒmen".
example.english: In Shanghainese, "ni" is sometimes used to mean "we".
example.fact: 伲 reflects usage from Wu Chinese dialects like Shanghainese, where it can mean "we/us" — showing how a character can carry an entirely different, dialect-specific meaning from standard Mandarin.

components.note: 犭 (animal) marks 猬 as an animal.
胃 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 猬’s reading.

example.hanzi: 刺猬遇到危险时会缩成一团。
example.pinyin: Cìwei yùdào wēixiǎn shí huì suōchéng yī tuán.
example.english: When hedgehogs encounter danger, they curl into a ball.
example.fact: Hedgehogs (刺猬) protect themselves by curling into a tight, spiny ball when threatened — a defense so effective that few predators can get past it.

etymologyHint: A tiger's eye 虎 stone 王; 虎 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 王 here represents 玉 (jade) — marking 琥 as a jade/stone object.
虎 (hǔ) is pronounced identically to 琥’s reading.

example.hanzi: 这块琥珀里有一只小昆虫。
example.pinyin: Zhè kuài hǔpò lǐ yǒu yī zhī xiǎo kūnchóng.
example.english: There is a small insect inside this piece of amber.
example.fact: 琥珀 (hǔpò, "amber") is fossilized tree resin, and pieces containing perfectly preserved ancient insects have given scientists real anatomical data about creatures from tens of millions of years ago.

components.note: 歹 (death/bad) marks 殁 as relating to death.
殳 (shū) has diverged substantially in sound from mò, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 他在战争中殁于沙场。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhànzhēng zhōng mò yú shāchǎng.
example.english: He died on the battlefield during the war.
example.fact: 殁 is a formal, literary verb for "to die", typically reserved for solemn writing such as obituaries or historical records rather than everyday conversation, where 死 or 去世 are used instead.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蚩 as originally naming a worm or insect.
屮 shares the initial ch- with chī, though the vowel differs — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 蚩尤是中国古代传说中的部落首领。
example.pinyin: Chīyóu shì Zhōngguó gǔdài chuánshuō zhōng de bùluò shǒulǐng.
example.english: Chiyou is a tribal leader in ancient Chinese legend.
example.fact: 蚩 is best known today as part of the name 蚩尤 (Chīyóu), a legendary tribal leader said to have fought the Yellow Emperor (黄帝) at the Battle of Zhuolu, one of the earliest battles in Chinese mythology.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 泾 as a river name.

example.hanzi: 泾河和渭河在陕西交汇。
example.pinyin: Jīng Hé hé Wèi Hé zài Shǎnxī jiāohuì.
example.english: The Jing River and the Wei River meet in Shaanxi.
example.fact: 泾 gives its name to the idiom 泾渭分明 (jīng wèi fēnmíng, "as clear as the Jing and Wei rivers"): where the muddy Jing and the clear Wei merge, their waters visibly stay separate for a stretch — the idiom describes something being sharply, unmistakably distinct.

meanings: used in 縹渺|缥渺[piao1 miao3]

components.note: 纟 (silk) marks 缥 as relating to silk — originally a shade of light blue silk.
票 (piào) is close to piāo’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 天边飘着缥缈的云彩。
example.pinyin: Tiānbiān piāo zhe piāomiǎo de yúncai.
example.english: Hazy, ethereal clouds float at the horizon.
example.fact: 缥 pairs with 缈 in 缥缈 (piāomiǎo), a word describing something hazy or dreamlike — often used in classical poetry to depict misty mountains or an otherworldly atmosphere.

meanings: to prepare a dead body for coffin

components.note: 歹 (death/bad) marks 殓 as relating to death and funeral rites.
佥 (qiān) has diverged substantially in sound from liàn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 家人为逝者举行了入殓仪式。
example.pinyin: Jiārén wèi shìzhě jǔxíngle rùliàn yíshì.
example.english: The family held the encoffining ceremony for the deceased.
example.fact: 殓 appears in 入殓 (rùliàn), the traditional Chinese funeral rite of dressing and placing the deceased into the coffin — a solemn ceremony that many families still follow with specific customary steps.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) marks 鳅 as a fish.
秋 (qiū) gives the sound — an exact match with 鳅’s reading.

example.hanzi: 泥鳅生活在稻田和池塘里。
example.pinyin: Níqiū shēnghuó zài dàotián hé chítáng lǐ.
example.english: Loaches live in rice paddies and ponds.
example.fact: 泥鳅 (níqiū, "loach") are small, slippery freshwater fish traditionally raised in Chinese rice paddies and prized in regional cuisine, especially in Jiangsu and Anhui.

components.note: 气 (gas) marks 氰 as originally naming a gas — cyanogen.
青 (qīng) is close to qíng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 氰化物是一种剧毒物质。
example.pinyin: Qínghuàwù shì yī zhǒng jùdú wùzhì.
example.english: Cyanide is a highly toxic substance.
example.fact: 氰 uses the gas radical 气 because cyanogen, the compound it originally named, is a colorless toxic gas; the character now more broadly refers to the cyanide (CN) group in chemistry, as in 氰化物 (qínghuàwù, "cyanide").

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 诋 as relating to spoken words — slander.
氐 (dī) is close to dǐ’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他被对手恶意诋毁。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi duìshǒu èyì dǐhuǐ.
example.english: He was maliciously slandered by his rival.
example.fact: 诋 appears in 诋毁 (dǐhuǐ), a common formal word for "to defame" or "to badmouth", frequently seen in news reports about defamation disputes.

components.note: ⺈ contributes a cutting sense — mowing grass for fodder.
彐 has diverged substantially in sound from chú, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 他提出的意见只是刍议，请多包涵。
example.pinyin: Tā tíchū de yìjiàn zhǐshì chúyì, qǐng duō bāohán.
example.english: The suggestions he raised are just my humble thoughts, please be understanding.
example.fact: 刍 appears in the self-deprecating phrase 刍议 (chúyì, literally "fodder-talk"), a modest way of describing one’s own opinion as being as lowly and unrefined as animal feed.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 芷 as a plant.
止 (zhǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 芷’s reading.

example.hanzi: 白芷是一种常用的中药材。
example.pinyin: Báizhǐ shì yī zhǒng chángyòng de zhōngyào cái.
example.english: Angelica root is a commonly used Chinese medicinal herb.
example.fact: 白芷 (báizhǐ, Angelica dahurica) is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb long used to relieve headaches and nasal congestion, and its fragrant root is also used as a spice.

components.note: 山 (mountain) marks 嶙 as relating to mountains and rocks.
粦 (lín) gives the sound — an exact match with 嶙’s reading.

example.hanzi: 那座山峰嶙峋陡峭。
example.pinyin: Nà zuò shānfēng línxún dòuqiào.
example.english: That mountain peak is jagged and steep.
example.fact: 嶙 pairs with 峋 in 嶙峋 (línxún), describing jagged, rugged mountain terrain — and by extension, a person’s gaunt, bony physique, as in 瘦骨嶙峋.

components.note: 辶 (walk) marks 逅 as relating to movement — an encounter while out and about.
后 (hòu) gives the sound — an exact match with 逅’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他们在旅途中邂逅了彼此。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài lǚtú zhōng xièhòu le bǐcǐ.
example.english: They encountered each other unexpectedly during their travels.
example.fact: 逅 exists solely in the compound 邂逅 (xièhòu), a poetic word for a chance, unexpected encounter — often used romantically in Chinese literature and film to describe fated meetings between strangers.

components.note: 舟 (boat) marks 舫 as a boat.
方 (fāng) is close to fǎng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 颐和园里有一座著名的石舫。
example.pinyin: Yíhéyuán lǐ yǒu yī zuò zhùmíng de shífǎng.
example.english: There is a famous stone boat in the Summer Palace.
example.fact: 石舫 ("the Marble Boat") is a famous stone boat-shaped pavilion in Beijing’s Summer Palace, popularly said to have been funded with money diverted from the imperial navy’s budget in the late 19th century — a story often cited in accounts of the Qing dynasty’s declining naval power.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 呓 as relating to speech — talking in one’s sleep.
艺 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 呓’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他昨晚说了梦呓。
example.pinyin: Tā zuówǎn shuōle mèngyì.
example.english: He talked in his sleep last night.
example.fact: 呓 exists mainly in 梦呓 (mèngyì, "to talk in one’s sleep"), and is used figuratively in modern Chinese to dismiss an unrealistic or delusional statement as mere "sleep-talk".

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 唰 as a sound.
刷 (shuā) gives the sound — an exact match with 唰’s reading.

example.hanzi: 雨"唰"地一下下起来了。
example.pinyin: Yǔ "shuā" de yīxià xià qǐlái le.
example.english: The rain suddenly poured down with a swishing sound.
example.fact: 唰 is a purely onomatopoeic character imitating a quick swishing or rushing sound, such as sudden rain, a curtain being drawn, or pages flipping rapidly.

etymologyHint: Sprouting 出 grass 艹; 出 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 茁 as relating to plants — sprouting.
出 (chū) shares its initial with zhuó, though the vowel and aspiration differ — a fairly loose match despite being listed as the phonetic element.

example.hanzi: 春天，麦苗茁壮成长。
example.pinyin: Chūntiān, màimiáo zhuózhuàng chéngzhǎng.
example.english: In spring, the wheat seedlings grow strong and healthy.
example.fact: 茁 appears almost exclusively in 茁壮 (zhuózhuàng, "healthy and vigorous"), so closely tied to describing thriving plants and children that Chinese textbooks often use the set phrase 茁壮成长 ("to grow up healthy and strong").

meanings: time of famine or crop failure
etymologyHint: A time of little 堇 food 饣; 堇 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 (food) marks 馑 as relating to food — or the lack of it.
堇 (jǐn) is pronounced identically to 馑’s reading.

example.hanzi: 古代常有饥馑之年。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài cháng yǒu jījǐn zhī nián.
example.english: Ancient times often had years of famine.
example.fact: 馑 pairs with 饥 in 饥馑 (jījǐn), a formal literary term for severe famine — historically a major concern in Chinese governance, with granaries and famine-relief systems built specifically to prevent such crises.

example.hanzi: 妫水河流经北京延庆。
example.pinyin: Guī Shuǐ Hé liújīng Běijīng Yánqìng.
example.english: The Gui River flows through Yanqing, Beijing.
example.fact: 妫 survives mainly as a surname and in the name of the Gui River (妫水河) in Yanqing, Beijing — the site of the 2019 Beijing International Horticultural Exhibition.

components.note: 马 (horse) marks 骧 as relating to horses.
襄 (xiāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 骧’s reading.

example.hanzi: 那匹马昂首骧腾，十分神气。
example.pinyin: Nà pǐ mǎ ángshǒu xiāngténg, shífēn shénqì.
example.english: That horse raised its head and reared up, looking very spirited.
example.fact: 骧 belongs to a group of rare literary characters coined specifically to describe fine details of horse behavior — once a socially important subject in aristocratic and military life.

etymologyHint: A sweet 甘 plant 艹; 甘 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 苷 as a plant-derived substance.
甘 (gān) is pronounced identically to 苷’s reading.

example.hanzi: 甘草苷是从甘草中提取的一种化合物。
example.pinyin: Gāncǎogān shì cóng gāncǎo zhōng tíqǔ de yī zhǒng huàhéwù.
example.english: Glycyrrhizin is a compound extracted from licorice.
example.fact: 苷 is the standard character for "glycoside" in modern Chinese chemistry, used for compounds found in many medicinal plants — its 甘 ("sweet") phonetic root reflects licorice’s naturally sweet taste.

components.note: 扌 (hand) marks 擢 as an action done with the hand — pulling up, selecting.
隹 (zhuī) shares the initial and tone with zhuó, though the vowel differs — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 他因才能出众被提擢为经理。
example.pinyin: Tā yīn cáinéng chūzhòng bèi tízhuó wéi jīnglǐ.
example.english: He was promoted to manager because of his outstanding ability.
example.fact: 擢 appears in the formal terms 擢升 (zhuóshēng) and 提擢 (tízhuó), both meaning "to promote" — used in official, written contexts about career advancement rather than everyday spoken Chinese.

meanings: ranges of hills stretching on beyond another irregular peaks

components.note: 山 (mountain) marks 峋 as relating to mountains and rocks.
旬 (xún) gives the sound — an exact match with 峋’s reading.

example.hanzi: 老人瘦得嶙峋，看上去很虚弱。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén shòu de línxún, kàn shàngqù hěn xūruò.
example.english: The old man was so thin his bones showed — he looked very frail.
example.fact: 峋 essentially only appears combined with 嶙 in 嶙峋 — like many Chinese characters, it has become so tied to one specific compound that it is rarely, if ever, used alone in modern writing.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) marks 袂 as an item of clothing — a sleeve.
夬 (guài) has diverged substantially in sound from mèi, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 她挥了挥衣袂，转身离去。
example.pinyin: Tā huī le huī yī mèi, zhuǎnshēn lí qù.
example.english: She waved her sleeve and turned to leave.
example.fact: 袂 is a literary, classical word for "sleeve", largely replaced by 袖子 (xiùzi) in modern speech — it survives mainly in set phrases like 联袂 (liánmèi, literally "joined sleeves", meaning "jointly", as when artists collaborate).

etymologyHint: With a heavy 满 heart 心; 满 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 心 (heart) marks 懑 as an emotional state — sorrow.
满 (mǎn) shares its initial with mèn, though the vowel and tone differ — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 他心中愤懑，却无处发泄。
example.pinyin: Tā xīnzhōng fènmèn, què wú chù fāxiè.
example.english: He was full of resentment inside, but had no outlet for it.
example.fact: 懑 pairs with 愤 in 愤懑 (fènmèn), a formal literary term describing bottled-up indignation — often used to describe someone who feels wronged but cannot openly protest.

meanings: rain coat made of straw etc

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 蓑 as made from plant material — a straw raincoat.
衰 is read shuāi in modern Mandarin, which no longer resembles suō — the phonetic connection reflects an older stage of the language now obscured by sound change.

example.hanzi: 渔夫披着蓑衣，在雨中捕鱼。
example.pinyin: Yúfū pīzhe suōyī, zài yǔ zhōng bǔ yú.
example.english: The fisherman wore a straw raincoat, fishing in the rain.
example.fact: 蓑衣 (suōyī) is a traditional Chinese raincoat woven from straw or palm fiber, worn by farmers and fishermen before rubber and plastic raincoats existed — it appears often in classical landscape poetry as a symbol of the reclusive fisherman.

example.hanzi: 他没有参與这次讨论。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu cānyù zhè cì tǎolùn.
example.english: He did not participate in this discussion.
example.fact: 與/与 is polyphonic: pronounced yǔ in words like 与 ("and, with"), but yù in words like 参与 (cānyù, "to participate") and 与会 (yùhuì, "to attend a meeting").

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 涞 as a river name.
来 (lái) gives the sound — an exact match with 涞’s reading.

example.hanzi: 涞水是河北的一个县。
example.pinyin: Láishuǐ shì Héběi de yī gè xiàn.
example.english: Laishui is a county in Hebei.
example.fact: 涞 appears in the names of two Hebei counties, 涞水 (Laishui) and 涞源 (Laiyuan), both in the mountainous region west of Beijing that historically guarded key routes into the capital.

components.note: 礻 (spirit/altar) marks 祉 as relating to blessings from the spirits.
止 (zhǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 祉’s reading.

example.hanzi: 祝愿大家福祉安康。
example.pinyin: Zhùyuàn dàjiā fúzhǐ ānkāng.
example.english: Wishing everyone happiness and well-being.
example.fact: 祉 appears in 福祉 (fúzhǐ, "well-being, welfare"), a formal term commonly used today in government and NGO language about public welfare policy.

components.note: 足 (foot) marks 踹 as an action done with the foot.
耑 (duān) has diverged substantially in sound from chuài, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 他一脚踹开了门。
example.pinyin: Tā yī jiǎo chuàikāile mén.
example.english: He kicked the door open with one kick.
example.fact: 踹 specifically describes a forceful kick using the sole or heel of the foot, distinct from 踢 (tī), the general word for "to kick" — Chinese action films often use 踹 for powerful, flat-footed kicks.

meanings: to pick up; to collect; to gather up

components.note: 扌 (hand) marks 掇 as an action done with the hand — picking up.
叕 (zhuó) has diverged substantially in sound from duō, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 他把地上的碎片一一掇起来。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ dìshàng de suìpiàn yīyī duō qǐlái.
example.english: He picked up the fragments on the ground one by one.
example.fact: 掇 appears in the colloquial phrase 拾掇 (shíduo), a northern Mandarin term meaning "to tidy up" or "to fix", commonly heard in everyday speech in and around Beijing.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 沏 as an action involving water — brewing.
切 (qiè) shares the initial q- with qī, though the vowel and tone differ — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 奶奶每天早上都要沏一壶茶。
example.pinyin: Nǎinai měitiān zǎoshang dōu yào qī yī hú chá.
example.english: Grandma brews a pot of tea every morning.
example.fact: 沏茶 (qīchá, "to brew tea") refers specifically to the traditional method of pouring hot water directly over tea leaves — a core step in the Chinese tea ceremony.

etymologyHint: Mad 狂 speech 讠; 狂 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 诳 as relating to spoken words — deceiving.
狂 (kuáng) is pronounced identically to 诳’s reading.

example.hanzi: 你不要再诳骗我了。
example.pinyin: Nǐ bùyào zài kuāngpiàn wǒ le.
example.english: Don’t deceive me anymore.
example.fact: 诳 combines with 骗 in 诳骗 (kuāngpiàn, "to deceive") and appears in the Buddhist term 诳语 (kuāngyǔ, "false speech") — one of the forms of wrong speech traditionally warned against in Buddhist ethical teaching.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 噫 as an interjection — a sound made with the mouth.
意 (yì) is close to yī’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: "噫！这是怎么回事？"他惊讶地说。
example.pinyin: "Yī! Zhè shì zěnme huí shì?" tā jīngyà de shuō.
example.english: "Oh! What is going on?" he said in surprise.
example.fact: 噫 is a classical interjection expressing surprise or sorrow, appearing famously in the closing line of Fan Zhongyan’s Song-dynasty essay "Yueyang Tower": "噫!微斯人,吾谁与归?" ("Alas! Without such a person, who could I follow?")

components.note: 饣 (food) marks 饽 as relating to food.
孛 is close to bō’s reading, sharing the initial and vowel and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 老北京人爱吃饽饽。
example.pinyin: Lǎo Běijīngrén ài chī bōbo.
example.english: Old Beijing residents love eating baked goods.
example.fact: 饽饽 (bōbo) is an old Beijing and northern Chinese term for baked goods like buns, cakes, or pastries — used broadly for wheat-flour foods before more specific modern terms became common.

components.note: 饣 (food) marks 饪 as relating to food — cooking.
壬 (rén) is close to rèn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她的烹饪技术非常好。
example.pinyin: Tā de pēngrèn jìshù fēicháng hǎo.
example.english: Her cooking skills are excellent.
example.fact: 饪 exists today almost solely in 烹饪 (pēngrèn), the standard formal word for "cooking" or "culinary arts", widely used in cookbook titles and professional culinary contexts.

etymologyHint: A wrinkle 咎 in a silk 纟 garment; 纟 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) reflects that 绺 names a thin, strand-like bundle — a tuft of hair or a skein of thread.

example.hanzi: 她剪下一绺头发留作纪念。
example.pinyin: Tā jiǎnxià yī liǔ tóufa liú zuò jìniàn.
example.english: She cut off a lock of hair to keep as a memento.
example.fact: 绺 functions as a measure word for a strand or lock of something thread-like, most often hair, as in 一绺头发 ("a lock of hair") — a good example of how Chinese uses different measure words for different shapes of objects.

etymologyHint: To discuss 讠 a plan 咨; 咨 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 谘 as relating to spoken words — consulting.
咨 (zī) is pronounced identically to 谘’s reading (谘 is itself essentially a variant built by adding 讠 to 咨).

example.hanzi: 遇到问题，可以向专家谘询。
example.pinyin: Yù dào wèntí, kěyǐ xiàng zhuānjiā zīxún.
example.english: When you run into a problem, you can consult an expert.
example.fact: 谘 is a variant of 咨, both used in 咨询/谘询 (zīxún, "to consult") — Hong Kong and Taiwan tend to prefer the 讠+咨 form, while mainland China standardized on the simpler 咨询.

etymologyHint: An evening 夕 meal 食

components.note: 夕 (evening) marks the time of day.
食 (food/meal) combines with 夕 to give the direct meaning "evening meal".

example.hanzi: 一粥一飧，当思来处不易。
example.pinyin: Yī zhōu yī sūn, dāng sī láichù bùyì.
example.english: For every bowl of porridge and every meal, one should remember how hard they were to come by.
example.fact: 飧 appears in the well-known line from Zhu Bolu’s Family Maxims (朱子家训), a Qing-dynasty text on frugality: "一粥一飧,当思来处不易" — a widely quoted teaching on gratitude for food.

meanings: used in personal names and place names

components.note: 辶 (walk) marks 迳 as relating to movement — passing by, going directly.

example.hanzi: 你可以迳自离开，不必等我。
example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ jìngzì líkāi, bùbì děng wǒ.
example.english: You can leave directly, no need to wait for me.
example.fact: 迳 functions as a variant of 径, most often seen today in the formal adverb 迳自 (jìngzì, "directly, on one’s own initiative"), used in official or written Chinese to describe acting without seeking permission first.

meanings: sickle for cutting grass or hay
to chop using this type of guillotine
etymologyHint: A metal 钅 knife 刂; 则 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 铡 as a metal blade.
则 (zé) has diverged substantially in sound from zhá, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 铡草机可以快速切碎饲料。
example.pinyin: Zhácǎojī kěyǐ kuàisù qiēsuì sìliào.
example.english: A fodder chopper can quickly chop up feed.
example.fact: 铡 refers to a traditional guillotine-style chopping blade historically used for cutting hay, and in popular legend, as an instrument of capital punishment — the "dog-head guillotine" (狗头铡) associated with folk-hero judge Bao Zheng (包公) in Chinese opera.

meanings: used in 雞樅|鸡枞[ji1 zong1]

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 枞 as a tree.
从 (cóng) is close to cōng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 枞树是一种常绿针叶树。
example.pinyin: Cōngshù shì yī zhǒng chánglǜ zhēnyèshù.
example.english: Fir trees are a type of evergreen coniferous tree.
example.fact: 枞 also names 枞阳县 (Zongyang County) in Anhui — but there the character is read zōng, a different tone from cōng used for "fir tree", a common pattern where place names preserve a distinct pronunciation.

components.note: 火 (fire) marks 熨 as relating to heat — ironing.
尉 (wèi) has diverged substantially in sound from yùn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 妈妈在熨衣服。
example.pinyin: Māma zài yùn yīfu.
example.english: Mom is ironing clothes.
example.fact: 熨 is polyphonic: read yùn it means "to iron" (熨衣服), but read yù it appears in 熨帖 (yùtiē), meaning "apt, fitting" or "comfortable" — a single character shifting pronunciation along with its meaning.

components.note: 金 (metal/gold) marks 鋈 as relating to metal — silver plating.
沃 (wò) is close to wù’s reading, sharing the initial and a related vowel.

example.hanzi: 古代战车上常有鋈饰的部件。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài zhànchē shàng cháng yǒu wùshì de bùjiàn.
example.english: Ancient war chariots often had silver-plated fittings.
example.fact: 鋈 is an extremely rare classical character describing silver- or tin-plated metal, appearing in the Book of Songs (诗经) — China’s oldest poetry anthology — in descriptions of ornamented chariot fittings.

meanings: used in 葒草|荭草[hong2 cao3]

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 荭 as a plant.
红 (hóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 荭’s reading.

example.hanzi: 荭草生长在河边湿地。
example.pinyin: Hóngcǎo shēngzhǎng zài hébiān shīdì.
example.english: Hong grass grows in wetlands by rivers.
example.fact: 荭草 ("prince’s feather", a type of smartweed) is a wetland plant whose Chinese name directly reflects its reddish flower spikes — 红 (hóng, "red") does double duty here as both color descriptor and phonetic component.

meanings: to buy or sell on credit

components.note: 贝 (money/shell) marks 赊 as relating to money — buying on credit.
佘 (shé) is close to shē’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 老板不同意让他赊账。
example.pinyin: Lǎobǎn bù tóngyì ràng tā shēzhàng.
example.english: The boss didn’t agree to let him buy on credit.
example.fact: 赊 appears in 赊账 (shēzhàng, "to buy on credit"), a practice long common in small Chinese shops before modern banking, where regular customers could pay their tab later, often recorded in a physical ledger.

etymologyHint: Someone 亻 with you all your life 寿; 寿 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 俦 as relating to a person — a companion.
寿 (shòu) shares the final -ou with chóu, though the initial and tone differ — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 志同道合的朋友才是真正的俦侣。
example.pinyin: Zhìtóngdàohé de péngyou cái shì zhēnzhèng de chóulǚ.
example.english: Friends who share the same ideals are true companions.
example.fact: 俦 is a literary word for "companion" or "peer", seen in formal compounds like 俦侣 — today largely replaced by 伙伴 or 同伴 in everyday speech.

meanings: used in 戛納|戛纳[Ga1 na4]
etymologyHint: To strike 戈 someone on the nose 自

components.note: 戈 (a dagger-axe weapon) depicts striking — matching 戛’s core sense of "to strike lightly".
自 is traditionally explained as representing a face being struck in the character’s ancient pictographic form, though the exact original structure is debated.

example.hanzi: 戛纳电影节每年都吸引众多明星。
example.pinyin: Jiánà Diànyǐngjié měinián dōu xīyǐn zhòngduō míngxīng.
example.english: The Cannes Film Festival attracts many stars every year.
example.fact: 戛 is best known today for its use in transliterating "Cannes" as 戛纳 (Jiánà), as in 戛纳电影节 (the Cannes Film Festival) — a case of a rare classical character finding new life as a phonetic loan for a foreign place name.

etymologyHint: A man's face 面 after drinking 氵; 面 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water/liquid) marks 湎 as relating to drinking.
面 (miàn) is close to miǎn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他终日沉湎于酒色之中。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngrì chénmiǎn yú jiǔsè zhī zhōng.
example.english: He indulges himself all day in drink and women.
example.fact: 湎 exists almost exclusively in 沉湎 (chénmiǎn), meaning "to be addicted to" or "indulge excessively in" — used for any overwhelming habit, as in 沉湎于网络游戏 ("addicted to online games").

example.hanzi: 电话号码里的"1"有时读作"幺"。
example.pinyin: Diànhuà hàomǎ lǐ de "1" yǒushí dú zuò "yāo".
example.english: The "1" in phone numbers is sometimes read as "yao".
example.fact: In spoken Chinese, 幺 is used instead of 一 (yī) when reading out digit strings like phone numbers, specifically to avoid confusion with other similar-sounding numbers when spoken quickly — similar to how English speakers might say "niner" for "nine" over a radio.

components.note: 冫 (ice) marks 凇 as relating to ice.
松 (sōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 凇’s reading.

example.hanzi: 冬天，树枝上结满了雾凇。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān, shùzhī shàng jié mǎnle wùsōng.
example.english: In winter, the tree branches are covered with rime ice.
example.fact: 雾凇 (wùsōng, "rime ice") is a famous winter phenomenon in Jilin province, where supercooled fog freezes onto trees creating frost-covered "ice trees" — the city of Jilin holds an annual festival to celebrate it.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 芪 as a plant.
氏 (shì) has diverged substantially in sound from qí, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 黄芪是一种补气的中药。
example.pinyin: Huángqí shì yī zhǒng bǔqì de zhōngyào.
example.english: Astragalus is a qi-tonifying Chinese medicinal herb.
example.fact: 黄芪 (huángqí, astragalus root) is one of the most commonly used herbs in traditional Chinese medicine, often added to soups and teas, and it is also studied in modern research for potential immune-supporting properties.

components.note: 角 (horn) marks 觯 as an object made from horn — a drinking vessel.
单 (dān) has diverged substantially in sound from zhì, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 博物馆展出了一件商代青铜觯。
example.pinyin: Bówùguǎn zhǎnchūle yī jiàn Shāngdài qīngtóng zhì.
example.english: The museum displayed a bronze "zhi" vessel from the Shang dynasty.
example.fact: 觯 names an ancient bronze wine vessel used in Shang and Zhou dynasty rituals, one of several specialized vessel-name characters — along with 爵, 尊, and 觥 — that reflect how elaborate ceremonial drinking was in early Chinese aristocratic culture.

components.note: 齿 (teeth) marks 龌 as relating to the mouth/teeth, part of the shared radical across both characters of 龌龊.
屋 (wū) shares the initial and a similar vowel with wò, though the exact vowel and tone differ — a moderate match.

example.hanzi: 那个房间又窄又龌龊。
example.pinyin: Nàge fángjiān yòu zhǎi yòu wòchuò.
example.english: That room is both cramped and filthy.
example.fact: 龌龊 (wòchuò) originally described something physically cramped and filthy; in modern Chinese it is now used almost entirely figuratively, for morally low or underhanded behavior.

components.note: 扌 (hand) marks 挞 as an action done by hand — flogging.
达 (dá) is close to tà’s reading — same final and tone, with a related initial.

example.hanzi: 老师不应该体罚或鞭挞学生。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī bù yìng gāi tǐfá huò biāntà xuésheng.
example.english: Teachers should not physically punish or whip students.
example.fact: 挞 appears in 鞭挞 (biāntà), literally "to whip" but used figuratively in modern Chinese media to mean "to sharply criticize or condemn", as in headlines that "鞭挞" corruption.

meanings: old variant of 贏|赢[ying2], to win, to profit

components.note: 女 (woman) marks 嬴 as an ancient clan-name character — several early Chinese surnames (姬, 姜, 嬴) carry this radical, reflecting very early matrilineal clan-naming traditions.

example.hanzi: 秦始皇姓嬴，名政。
example.pinyin: Qín Shǐhuáng xìng Yíng, míng Zhèng.
example.english: Qin Shi Huang’s surname was Ying, given name Zheng.
example.fact: 嬴 was the surname of the royal house of Qin, making it the family name of Qin Shi Huang (嬴政), the first emperor to unify China in 221 BCE.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 苻 as a plant.
付 (fù) is close to fú’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 苻坚是前秦的著名君主。
example.pinyin: Fú Jiān shì Qián Qín de zhùmíng jūnzhǔ.
example.english: Fu Jian was a famous ruler of the Former Qin dynasty.
example.fact: 苻 is best known as the surname of Fu Jian (苻坚), the ambitious 4th-century ruler who briefly unified most of northern China before his defeat at the Battle of Fei River in 383 CE.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 嘁 as a sound.
戚 (qī) gives the sound — an exact match with 嘁’s reading.

example.hanzi: 大家嘁嘁喳喳地讨论起来。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā qīqīchāchā de tǎolùn qǐlái.
example.english: Everyone started discussing in hushed, chattering voices.
example.fact: 嘁 appears in 嘁嘁喳喳 (qīqīchāchā), an onomatopoeia for the sound of people whispering or chattering among themselves, often with a slightly negative, gossipy connotation.

components.note: 革 (leather) marks 鞯 as a leather object — a saddle blanket.
荐 (jiàn) is close to jiān’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 马鞍下垂着一层鞍鞯。
example.pinyin: Mǎ’ān xià chuízhe yī céng ān jiān.
example.english: A saddle blanket hangs beneath the saddle.
example.fact: 鞯 appears in 鞍鞯 (ānjiān), the padded blanket placed beneath a horse’s saddle — this exact phrase appears in the classic poem "Ballad of Mulan": "东市买鞍鞯" ("At the eastern market she bought a saddle blanket").

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks 肽 as relating to the body — a biochemical compound.
太 (tài) gives the sound — an exact match with 肽’s reading.

example.hanzi: 蛋白质是由多个肽链组成的。
example.pinyin: Dànbáizhì shì yóu duō gè tàiliàn zǔchéng de.
example.english: Proteins are made up of multiple peptide chains.
example.fact: 肽 is a modern scientific coinage combining the flesh/body radical ⺼ with the phonetic 太 (tài) to transliterate "peptide" — part of a wave of 20th-century Chinese characters created specifically for biochemistry.

etymologyHint: Moving 动 and sad 忄; 动 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart) marks 恸 as an emotional state — grief.
动 (dòng) shares the final -ong and tone with tòng, differing only in the initial — a close match.

example.hanzi: 听到噩耗，全家人都恸哭不已。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào èhào, quánjiārén dōu tòngkū bùyǐ.
example.english: Hearing the terrible news, the whole family wept in grief without stopping.
example.fact: 恸 describes grief beyond ordinary sadness — it appears in the Analects of Confucius describing his uncontrollable weeping (恸哭) upon the death of his beloved disciple Yan Hui, one of the few times classical texts show Confucius losing his composure.

components.note: 辶 (walk) contributes an abstract sense of progression through time.
台 (tái) shares the final -ai with dài, though the initial and tone differ — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 迨至天明，雨才停了。
example.pinyin: Dài zhì tiānmíng, yǔ cái tíngle.
example.english: It wasn’t until dawn that the rain finally stopped.
example.fact: 迨 is a classical Chinese conjunction meaning "until" or "by the time that", now confined to formal literary writing — in everyday modern speech, 等到 or 直到 are used instead.

etymologyHint: A treasure of gold 钅 and jade 玉; 玉 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 钰 as a valuable metal or treasure.
玉 (yù) is pronounced identically to 钰’s reading.

example.hanzi: "钰"这个字常用于女孩的名字。
example.pinyin: "Yù" zhège zì cháng yòngyú nǚhái de míngzi.
example.english: The character "yu" is often used in girls’ names.
example.fact: 钰 is used almost exclusively as a personal name character in modern Chinese, chosen by parents for its meaning of "precious treasure" — combining metal and jade, two classically valued materials.

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 儆 as relating to a person’s action — warning.
敬 (jìng) is close to jǐng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 政府杀一儆百，严惩了这起腐败案。
example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ shā yī jǐng bǎi, yánchéngle zhè qǐ fǔbài àn.
example.english: The government punished this corruption case severely, executing one as a warning to a hundred.
example.fact: 儆 appears in the idiom 杀一儆百 (shā yī jǐng bǎi, "kill one to warn a hundred"), describing exemplary punishment meant to deter others — still commonly used today in discussions of law enforcement.

components.note: 见 (to see) marks 觎 as relating to desiring something in view.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 觎’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他对公司的财产早有觊觎之心。
example.pinyin: Tā duì gōngsī de cáichǎn zǎo yǒu jìyú zhī xīn.
example.english: He has long harbored covetous designs on the company’s assets.
example.fact: 觎 exists solely in 觊觎 (jìyú), a formal literary term for coveting something that belongs to someone else, especially power or position — frequently used in writing about ambitious rivals.

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 讫 as relating to a formal statement — completion, finishing.
乞 (qǐ) is close to qì’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 合同已经履行完讫。
example.pinyin: Hétong yǐjīng lǚxíng wán qì.
example.english: The contract has already been fully carried out.
example.fact: 讫 appears in formal business and legal Chinese, such as 付讫 (fùqì, "payment completed") or 收讫 (shōuqì, "received"), both commonly stamped on official receipts and invoices.

components.note: 氵 (water/liquid) marks 滓 as relating to a liquid’s residue — dregs.
宰 (zǎi) has diverged substantially in sound from zǐ, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 咖啡过滤后会留下一些渣滓。
example.pinyin: Kāfēi guòlǜ hòu huì liúxià yīxiē zhāzǐ.
example.english: After coffee is filtered, some dregs are left behind.
example.fact: 滓 pairs with 渣 in 渣滓 (zhāzǐ), meaning "dregs" or "sediment", and by extension is used figuratively in Chinese to describe worthless, contemptible people, as in calling someone "社会渣滓" ("dregs of society").

meanings: old variant of 壯|壮, Zhuang ethnic group of Guangxi
etymologyHint: A servant boy 童; 童 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 僮 as relating to a person — a boy servant.
童 (tóng) is pronounced identically to 僮’s reading.

example.hanzi: 古代富贵人家常有书僮伺候。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài fùguì rénjiā cháng yǒu shūtóng cìhòu.
example.english: Wealthy families in ancient times often had a young study attendant in service.
example.fact: 僮 was historically also used to write the name of the Zhuang ethnic group (now written 壮族, Zhuàngzú), China’s largest minority group — the character was officially changed in 1965, partly to remove 僮’s "servant/child" connotation.

etymologyHint: To know a woman's 女 secret 冓; 冓 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 (woman) marks 媾 as relating to marriage.
冓 (gòu) is pronounced identically to 媾’s reading.

example.hanzi: 两国终于媾和，结束了战争。
example.pinyin: Liǎng guó zhōngyú gòuhé, jiéshùle zhànzhēng.
example.english: The two countries finally made peace, ending the war.
example.fact: 媾 appears in the formal term 媾和 (gòuhé), meaning "to make peace" between warring parties — usually reserved for diplomatic and historical writing about treaty negotiations.

components.note: 齿 (teeth) marks 龇 as relating to the teeth.
此 (cǐ) shares a similar sibilant quality with zī, though the exact sound has diverged.

example.hanzi: 那只狗龇牙咧嘴地叫着。
example.pinyin: Nà zhī gǒu zīyá liězuǐ de jiàozhe.
example.english: That dog barked, baring its teeth.
example.fact: 龇 appears in 龇牙咧嘴 (zīyá liězuǐ), a vivid four-character idiom describing a snarling, teeth-baring expression, used for both angry animals and people grimacing in pain or fury.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks 胯 as relating to a body part — the hip.
夸 (kuā) is close to kuà’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他的胯部在运动中受了伤。
example.pinyin: Tā de kuàbù zài yùndòng zhōng shòule shāng.
example.english: He injured his hip area during exercise.
example.fact: 胯 refers specifically to the hip/groin area where the leg joins the torso, and appears in 胯下 (kuàxià, "between the legs") — including in the well-known story of the young Han Xin (韩信) enduring the humiliation of crawling between a bully’s legs before becoming one of China’s greatest generals.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 涮 as relating to water — rinsing, quick-boiling.
刷 (shuā) is close to shuàn’s reading, sharing the initial and a related final.

example.hanzi: 我们冬天喜欢吃涮羊肉。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dōngtiān xǐhuan chī shuàn yángròu.
example.english: We like eating hot-pot mutton in winter.
example.fact: 涮羊肉 (shuàn yángròu, "instant-boiled mutton") is the classic Beijing hot pot dish where thin slices of mutton are swished briefly in boiling broth — the character 涮 literally captures that quick swishing motion.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) marks 绾 as relating to twisting or binding thread-like material — hair.
官 (guān) has diverged substantially in sound from wǎn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 她把头发绾成一个发髻。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ tóufa wǎnchéng yī gè fàjì.
example.english: She coiled her hair up into a bun.
example.fact: 绾 describes the traditional method of twisting and pinning up long hair into a bun (绾发), a common hairstyle throughout imperial Chinese history for both men and women.

etymologyHint: Where two branches 木 fork 叉; 叉 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 杈 as a wooden tool made from a forked branch.
叉 (chā) is pronounced identically to 杈’s reading.

example.hanzi: 农民用木杈翻晒麦秸。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng mùchā fānshài màijiē.
example.english: Farmers use a wooden pitchfork to turn and dry wheat straw.
example.fact: 杈 names a traditional wooden farm tool shaped like a forked branch, used for centuries to turn and gather hay before mechanized farm equipment became common.

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) marks 赳 as relating to a vigorous, marching bearing.
丩 (jiū) gives the sound — an exact match with 赳’s reading.

example.hanzi: 士兵们赳赳雄壮地走过广场。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen jiūjiū xióngzhuàng de zǒuguò guǎngchǎng.
example.english: The soldiers marched grandly and imposingly across the square.
example.fact: 赳 appears only in the reduplicated form 赳赳, describing a vigorous, imposing bearing — it appears as early as the Book of Songs (诗经), in the line "赳赳武夫" ("a stalwart warrior"), one of the oldest surviving uses of the character.

meanings: dry measure equal to some five or ten dou (

components.note: 斗 (a measuring vessel) marks 斛 as a unit of measure.
角 (jiǎo) has diverged substantially in sound from hú, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 古代用斛来计量粮食。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài yòng hú lái jìliàng liángshí.
example.english: In ancient times, the "hu" was used to measure grain.
example.fact: 斛 was a traditional Chinese unit of dry volume, historically equal to ten 斗 (dou) — roughly 50 liters — used for centuries to measure grain in taxation and trade before the metric system was adopted.

meanings: a cup made of horn obstinate

components.note: 角 (horn) marks 觥 as an object made from horn — a drinking cup.
光 (guāng) shares the initial and tone with gōng, though the final differs — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 宴会上，大家觥筹交错，十分热闹。
example.pinyin: Yànhuì shàng, dàjiā gōngchóu jiāocuò, shífēn rènao.
example.english: At the banquet, cups and gaming pieces mingled everywhere — it was very lively.
example.fact: 觥 appears in the idiom 觥筹交错 (gōngchóu jiāocuò, "wine cups and game tallies mingle"), from the Song-dynasty essay "The Old Drunkard’s Pavilion" by Ouyang Xiu, describing the lively chaos of a banquet.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) marks 疸 as a medical condition.
旦 (dàn) is close to dǎn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 新生儿黄疸是很常见的现象。
example.pinyin: Xīnshēng’ér huángdǎn shì hěn chángjiàn de xiànxiàng.
example.english: Neonatal jaundice is a very common phenomenon.
example.fact: 黄疸 (huángdǎn, "jaundice") causes yellowing of the skin and eyes due to excess bilirubin, and is especially common in newborns — most cases resolve on their own within a couple of weeks as the infant’s liver matures.

example.hanzi: 卞和是历史上着名的和氏璧的发现者。
example.pinyin: Biàn Hé shì lìshǐ shàng zhùmíng de Héshìbì de fāxiànzhě.
example.english: Bian He was the historical figure who discovered the famed jade "Heshibi".
example.fact: 卞 is best known as the surname of Bian He (卞和), the legendary Chu-state figure who, according to tradition, discovered the famed jade 和氏璧 (Heshibi), a jewel said to have later been fashioned into China’s first imperial seal.

components.note: 忄 (heart) marks 愠 as an emotional state — anger.
昷 has diverged substantially in sound from yùn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 人不知而不愠，不亦君子乎？
example.pinyin: Rén bù zhī ér bù yùn, bù yì jūnzǐ hū?
example.english: Is it not the mark of a gentleman not to resent it when others fail to appreciate him?
example.fact: 愠 appears in one of the most famous opening lines of the Analects of Confucius — among the very first lines students of classical Chinese are asked to memorize.

components.note: 扌 (hand) contributes an abstract sense tied to effort and labor.
吉 (jí) is close to jié’s reading, sharing the initial and differing mainly in the vowel and tone.

example.hanzi: 他们家生活拮据，勉强维持温饱。
example.pinyin: Tāmen jiā shēnghuó jiéjū, miǎnqiǎng wéichí wēnbǎo.
example.english: Their family lives in financial hardship, barely managing to get by.
example.fact: 拮 exists almost solely in 拮据 (jiéjū), meaning "hard-pressed for money" — one of the most common ways in Chinese to describe being short on cash without sounding as blunt as 穷 ("poor").

components.note: 广 (shelter) marks 庠 as relating to a building — a school.
羊 (yáng) shares the tone with xiáng, though the exact sound differs — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 古代的"庠"相当于现在的地方学校。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài de "xiáng" xiāngdāng yú xiànzài de dìfang xuéxiào.
example.english: The ancient "xiang" was equivalent to today’s local school.
example.fact: 庠 was an ancient term for a local village school, appearing alongside 序 (xù) in 庠序 — a term Mencius used to describe the network of local schools he believed a good government should establish.

etymologyHint: A glorious 华 blaze 火; 华 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) marks 烨 as relating to fire and light — a blaze.

华 (splendor) is said to lend the sound in the source etymology, but its modern reading (huá) does not closely resemble yè — if a sound connection exists at all, it reflects an older stage of pronunciation, so it is treated here as a meaning contribution ("glorious") rather than a reliable phonetic.

example.hanzi: "烨"是一个寓意光明灿烂的常见人名用字。
example.pinyin: "Yè" shì yī gè yùyì guāngmíng cànlàn de chángjiàn rénmíng yòngzì.
example.english: "Ye" is a common character used in given names, symbolizing brightness and splendor.
example.fact: 烨 is used almost exclusively as a personal name character in modern Chinese, chosen for its bright, blazing imagery — it very rarely appears in ordinary vocabulary outside of names.

meanings: used in given names and as a surname

components.note: 龠 (a panpipe wind instrument) evokes harmonious music, the root sense behind "harmony".
禾 (hé) is pronounced identically to 龢’s reading.

example.hanzi: 龢字现在多用于人名。
example.pinyin: Hé zì xiànzài duō yòng yú rénmíng.
example.english: The character "he" (龢) is nowadays mostly used in given names.
example.fact: 龢 is an ancient variant of 和 (hé, "harmony"), combining 龠 (a panpipe instrument, evoking harmonious music) with the phonetic 禾. Though 和 replaced it in everyday use, 龢 still appears occasionally in personal names for its meaning of peace and harmony.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 菠 as a plant.
波 (bō) gives the sound — an exact match with 菠’s reading.

example.hanzi: 菠菜富含铁和维生素。
example.pinyin: Bōcài fùhán tiě hé wéishēngsù.
example.english: Spinach is rich in iron and vitamins.
example.fact: 菠菜 (bōcài, spinach) was introduced to China from the Persia/Nepal region during the Tang dynasty — the character 菠 was specifically coined to transliterate the plant’s foreign name upon its arrival.

components.note: 穴 (cave/hole) contributes a sense of seclusion, hiddenness.
幼 (yòu) has diverged substantially in sound from yǎo, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 窈窕淑女，君子好逑。
example.pinyin: Yǎotiǎo shūnǚ, jūnzǐ hǎo qiú.
example.english: A graceful, virtuous maiden — a fine gentleman would seek her hand.
example.fact: 窈 appears in 窈窕 (yǎotiǎo, "graceful, elegant"), famously used in the opening poem of the Book of Songs (诗经), China’s oldest poetry anthology.

components.note: 缶 (a clay vessel) marks 罄 as relating to an emptied container.
殸 is understood to read qìng in this context (related to 磬), giving an exact match with 罄’s reading.

example.hanzi: 家里粮食即将罄尽。
example.pinyin: Jiālǐ liángshí jíjiāng qìngjìn.
example.english: The food at home is about to run out completely.
example.fact: 罄 appears in the idiom 罄竹难书 (qìng zhú nán shū, "even using up all the bamboo [writing strips] could not record it all") — describing wrongdoings so numerous they defy full documentation, a reference to ancient bamboo-strip books.

components.note: 囗 (enclosure) marks 囤 as a container — a storage bin.
屯 (tún) is close to dùn’s reading — same final and tone, with a related initial.

example.hanzi: 疫情期间，很多人囤了大量口罩。
example.pinyin: Yìqíng qījiān, hěn duō rén dùnle dàliàng kǒuzhào.
example.english: During the pandemic, many people hoarded large quantities of masks.
example.fact: 囤 shifted from its original literal meaning of "a round grain storage bin" to the common modern verb 囤 (dùn, "to hoard/stockpile"), widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic to describe panic-buying.

meanings: conical cap worn during Zhou dynasty
military officer of low rank (in former times)
etymologyHint: Two hands 廾 putting the cap 厶 on someone's head

components.note: 厶 represents the cap itself in the character’s ancient pictographic form.
廾 (two hands) depicts hands placing the cap onto someone’s head.

example.hanzi: 弁是古代贵族戴的一种礼帽。
example.pinyin: Biàn shì gǔdài guìzú dài de yī zhǒng lǐmào.
example.english: "Bian" was a type of ceremonial cap worn by ancient nobles.
example.fact: 弁 named a ceremonial cap worn by nobles and officials in the Zhou dynasty; its meaning later extended to "preceding" (弁言, biànyán, "preface"), since a cap sits at the top/front of one’s attire, much like a preface sits at the front of a book.

components.note: 大 (big) marks 奘 as describing something large or stout.
壯 (zhuàng) shares the final -ang and tone with zàng, differing in the initial — a close match.

example.hanzi: 唐代高僧玄奘西行取经。
example.pinyin: Tángdài gāosēng Xuánzàng xīxíng qǔjīng.
example.english: The Tang-dynasty eminent monk Xuanzang traveled west to obtain Buddhist scriptures.
example.fact: 奘 is best known today as part of the name 玄奘 (Xuánzàng), the Tang-dynasty Buddhist monk whose 17-year overland journey to India inspired the classic novel Journey to the West (西游记).

meanings: the sound of large door closing

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 咣 as a sound.
光 (guāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 咣’s reading.

example.hanzi: 门"咣"的一声被风吹开了。
example.pinyin: Mén "guāng" de yī shēng bèi fēng chuīkāi le.
example.english: The door swung open with a bang from the wind.
example.fact: 咣 is a purely onomatopoeic character for a loud clanging or banging sound, most often a heavy door slamming — like many sound-effect characters, it carries the 口 ("mouth") radical.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) marks 缫 as relating to thread — reeling silk.
巢 (cháo) has diverged substantially in sound from sāo, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 古代妇女常在家中缫丝织布。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài fùnǚ cháng zài jiāzhōng sāosī zhībù.
example.english: Ancient women often reeled silk and wove cloth at home.
example.fact: 缫丝 (sāosī, "silk reeling") is the traditional process of unwinding continuous silk filament from boiled silkworm cocoons — a single cocoon can yield an unbroken thread of several hundred meters, sometimes over a kilometer.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks 腴 as relating to the body — plumpness, richness.
臾 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 腴’s reading.

example.hanzi: 这片土地十分肥腴，适合耕种。
example.pinyin: Zhè piàn tǔdì shífēn féiyú, shìhé gēngzhòng.
example.english: This land is very fertile, suitable for farming.
example.fact: 腴 pairs with 肥 in 肥腴 (féiyú), describing rich, fertile land or, in classical usage, a plump, well-fed appearance — both senses reflect the character’s core idea of abundance.

meanings: used in 縹緲|缥缈[piao1 miao3]
etymologyHint: A veil 纟 over the eyes 眇; 眇 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) marks 缈 as relating to a thin, veil-like quality — faintness.
眇 (miǎo) is pronounced identically to 缈’s reading.

example.hanzi: 她的歌声缥缈动听，仿佛来自仙境。
example.pinyin: Tā de gēshēng piāomiǎo dòngtīng, fǎngfú láizì xiānjìng.
example.english: Her singing was ethereal and lovely, as if it came from a fairyland.
example.fact: 缈 exists solely in 缥缈 (piāomiǎo, "faint, hazy, ethereal") — it and 缥 form one of Chinese’s many "bound" two-character words that almost never appear apart.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 喵 as a sound.
苗 (miáo) is close to miāo’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小猫喵喵地叫着要吃饭。
example.pinyin: Xiǎomāo miāomiāo de jiàozhe yào chīfàn.
example.english: The kitten meowed wanting to eat.
example.fact: 喵 has surged in everyday written usage thanks to internet cat culture, and is one of the clearest examples of an onomatopoeic character whose meaning is immediately intuitive even to non-native learners.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 潢 as relating to a body of water.
黄 (huáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 潢’s reading.

example.hanzi: 潢川是河南省的一个县。
example.pinyin: Huángchuān shì Hénán Shěng de yī gè xiàn.
example.english: Huangchuan is a county in Henan province.
example.fact: 潢 survives today mainly in the place name 潢川 (Huangchuan County) in Henan — a common pattern where obscure literary characters persist only because they are locked into a specific place name.

components.note: 辶 (walk) marks 遛 as relating to walking, strolling.
留 (liú) gives the sound — an exact match with 遛’s liú reading (used in the rarer word 逗遛); note that in everyday words like 遛狗, 遛 is instead read liù, a separate tone-differentiated reading.

example.hanzi: 爷爷每天早上都去公园遛狗。
