example.pinyin: Yéye měitiān zǎoshang dōu qù gōngyuán liù gǒu.
example.english: Grandpa walks the dog in the park every morning.
example.fact: 遛 is polyphonic: in the everyday words 遛狗 (liù gǒu, "to walk a dog") or 遛弯儿 (liù wànr, "to take a stroll"), it is read liù (4th tone) — the reading virtually all speakers use — while the rarer liú (2nd tone) reading appears only in the archaic word 逗遛 (dòuliú, "to loiter").

components.note: 木 (wood/tree) marks 柚 as a fruit tree.
由 (yóu) is close to yòu’s reading, differing only in tone — and yóu is itself 柚’s own alternate reading, used in 柚木 ("teak").

example.hanzi: 柚子酸甜可口，深受人们喜爱。
example.pinyin: Yòuzi suān tián kěkǒu, shēn shòu rénmen xǐ’ài.
example.english: Pomelos are tangy and sweet, much loved by people.
example.fact: 柚 is polyphonic: read yòu it names the pomelo fruit (柚子), but read yóu it appears in 柚木 (yóumù), the Chinese word for "teak" — and yóu happens to be the exact reading of its own phonetic component 由.

components.note: 阝 (place/mound) marks 郏 as a place name.
夹 (jiá) gives the sound — an exact match with 郏’s reading.

example.hanzi: 郏县是河南省的一个县。
example.pinyin: Jiáxiàn shì Hénán Shěng de yī gè xiàn.
example.english: Jiaxian is a county in Henan province.
example.fact: 郏县 (Jia County) in Henan is traditionally the burial place of the great Song-dynasty poet Su Dongpo (苏东坡), who requested to be laid to rest there.

meanings: used in Japanese names with phonetic value Ogi

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 荻 as a plant — a reed.
狄 (dí) gives the sound — an exact match with 荻’s reading.

example.hanzi: 秋天，河边长满了芦荻。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān, hébiān zhǎngmǎnle lúdí.
example.english: In autumn, the riverside is overgrown with reeds.
example.fact: 荻 names a reed plant related to 芦, and appears together with it in 芦荻 — evoking the classic autumn riverside imagery common in Chinese landscape poetry.

components.note: 艹 (grass) marks 藜 as a plant.
黎 (lí) gives the sound — an exact match with 藜’s reading.

example.hanzi: 藜麦是一种营养丰富的谷物。
example.pinyin: Límài shì yī zhǒng yíngyǎng fēngfù de gǔwù.
example.english: Quinoa is a nutrient-rich grain.
example.fact: 藜 is used to translate "quinoa" as 藜麦 (límài) in modern Chinese — a relatively recent borrowing, since quinoa only became widely known in China in the 21st century as a popular health food.

components.note: 王 here represents 玉 (jade) — marking 琨 as a type of fine stone.
昆 (kūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 琨’s reading.

example.hanzi: "琨"字常用于人名，寓意美玉。
example.pinyin: "Kūn" zì cháng yòngyú rénmíng, yùyì měiyù.
example.english: The character "kun" is often used in given names, symbolizing beautiful jade.
example.fact: 琨 is used almost exclusively as a personal name character today, valued for its meaning of fine jade — jade has held deep cultural significance in China for millennia, traditionally symbolizing virtue and moral integrity.

etymologyHint: A metal bit 钅 used to saddle 麃 a horse

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 镳 as a metal object — a horse’s bit.
麃 relates to a running animal, connecting to the idea of a horse being controlled and ridden.

example.hanzi: 分道扬镳，从此各奔前程。
example.pinyin: Fēndào yángbiāo, cóngcǐ gè bèn qiánchéng.
example.english: They part ways and go their separate paths from now on.
example.fact: 镳 exists almost solely in the idiom 分道扬镳 (fēndào yángbiāo, literally "to part roads and raise the bit"), meaning "to part ways" — the imagery comes from two riders whipping their horses’ bits to head off in different directions.

components.note: 隹 (short-tailed bird) marks 雉 as a bird.
矢 (shǐ) shares a retroflex-adjacent initial quality with zhì, though the vowel and tone differ — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 野鸡也叫雉，羽毛非常艳丽。
example.pinyin: Yějī yě jiào zhì, yǔmáo fēicháng yànlì.
example.english: Wild pheasants are also called "zhi" — their feathers are extremely brilliant.
example.fact: 雉 is the formal, classical name for the pheasant, a bird whose brilliantly colored feathers made it a recurring symbol of beauty in classical Chinese art and literature.

meanings: a bag opening at both ends

example.hanzi: 他倾其囊橐，资助贫困学生。
example.pinyin: Tā qīng qí nángtuó, zīzhù pínkùn xuésheng.
example.english: He emptied his savings to help support poor students.
example.fact: 橐 appears in 囊橐 (nángtuó), a classical term for one’s personal money bags. Laozi’s Daodejing uses a related image, comparing the space between heaven and earth to a bellows (橐龠, a bag-and-pipe device used to blow air into a fire).

etymologyHint: The place 阝 of the sun 昜; compare 阴

components.note: 阝 (a hill/mound) marks 陽 as relating to a landform.
昜 depicts the sun, giving 陽 its core meaning: the sunlit side of a landform.

example.hanzi: 山南水北谓之阳。
example.pinyin: Shān nán shuǐ běi wèi zhī yáng.
example.english: The south side of a mountain and the north bank of a river are called "yang".
example.fact: 陽/阳 (yáng) traditionally denoted the sunlit side of a landform — the south face of a mountain or north bank of a river — which is why so many Chinese place names contain 阳, such as 洛阳 (Luoyang) and 衡阳 (Hengyang).

meanings: (of a pair of horses) to pull side by side
etymologyHint: A team of horses 马 working together 并

components.note: 马 (horse) marks 骈 as relating to horses — a team working together.
并 (together, side by side) contributes the sense of pairing or parallel joining.

example.hanzi: 骈文讲究对仗工整。
example.pinyin: Piánwén jiǎngjiū duìzhàng gōngzhěng.
example.english: Parallel prose emphasizes neat, balanced parallelism.
example.fact: 骈 gives its name to 骈文 (piánwén, "parallel prose"), a highly stylized form of classical Chinese writing built from paired, balanced phrases — it dominated much literary composition during the Six Dynasties period before Tang writers pushed back toward plainer prose.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蛉 as an insect.
令 (lìng) is close to líng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 蜻蛉在水边飞舞。
example.pinyin: Qīnglíng zài shuǐbiān fēiwǔ.
example.english: Dragonflies flit about by the water’s edge.
example.fact: 蛉 appears in 蜻蛉, a classical/literary word for dragonfly, alongside the more common modern term 蜻蜓 — both refer to the same insect, but 蜻蛉 is more often found in poetry and older texts.

example.hanzi: 艮是八卦中代表山的卦。
example.pinyin: Gěn shì bāguà zhōng dàibiǎo shān de guà.
example.english: Gen is the trigram in the Eight Trigrams that represents mountain.
example.fact: 艮 is one of the Eight Trigrams (八卦) of the I Ching, representing "mountain" and the direction northeast — in colloquial Beijing Mandarin, the same character also means "tough" or "stubborn" when describing food texture or a person’s personality, an unrelated slang usage.

components.note: 扌 (hand) marks 搽 as an action done by hand — applying, rubbing on.
茶 (chá) gives the sound — an exact match with 搽’s reading.

example.hanzi: 她每天都会在脸上搽护肤霜。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān dōu huì zài liǎn shàng chá hùfū shuāng.
example.english: She applies moisturizer on her face every day.
example.fact: 搽 specifically describes smearing or rubbing a substance like lotion onto the skin — a more literary alternative to the everyday verb 抹 (mǒ), often seen on cosmetic product packaging.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 濡 as relating to water — moistening.
需 (xū) has diverged substantially in sound from rú, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 孩子从小耳濡目染，学会了书法。
example.pinyin: Háizi cóngxiǎo ěrrúmùrǎn, xuéhuìle shūfǎ.
example.english: Since childhood, the child absorbed the influence around him and learned calligraphy.
example.fact: 濡 appears in the idiom 耳濡目染 (ěrrúmùrǎn, literally "ears moistened, eyes dyed"), describing how a person absorbs habits or knowledge gradually through constant exposure rather than deliberate study.

components.note: 宀 (roof) marks 寮 as relating to a building — a hut.
尞 (liáo) gives the sound — an exact match with 寮’s reading.

example.hanzi: 山间有几间简陋的寮屋。
example.pinyin: Shānjiān yǒu jǐ jiān jiǎnlòu de liáowū.
example.english: There are a few crude huts among the mountains.
example.fact: 寮 appears in 寮屋 (liáowū), a term still used in Hong Kong for informal, self-built shanty structures — a housing issue the Hong Kong government has grappled with for decades because of land scarcity.

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 coffin 匛; 匛 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 柩 as a wooden object — a coffin.
匛 is understood to read jiù, giving an exact match with 柩’s reading.

example.hanzi: 灵柩缓缓地被抬出灵堂。
example.pinyin: Língjiù huǎnhuǎn de bèi tái chū língtáng.
example.english: The coffin was slowly carried out of the memorial hall.
example.fact: 柩 appears in 灵柩 (língjiù), the formal, respectful term for a coffin containing a body — used specifically for funeral contexts, distinct from 棺材 (guāncai), which can also refer to an empty coffin.

etymologyHint: Another 它 person 亻; see 他 and 她 for modern variants

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 佗 as relating to a person.
它 (tā) shares the initial t- with tuó, though the vowel and tone differ — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 华佗是中国古代著名的医学家。
example.pinyin: Huà Tuó shì Zhōngguó gǔdài zhùmíng de yīxuéjiā.
example.english: Hua Tuo was a famous physician in ancient China.
example.fact: 佗 is best known today as part of the name 华佗 (Huà Tuó), a legendary physician of the late Han dynasty credited as one of the earliest surgeons in Chinese medical history.

meanings: used in 啷當|啷当[lang1 dang1]

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 啷 as a sound.
郎 (láng) is close to lāng’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 钥匙叮叮啷啷地响。
example.pinyin: Yàoshi dīngdīng lāngláng de xiǎng.
example.english: The keys jingled and rattled.
example.fact: 啷 typically appears paired with 当 in 当啷 (dānglāng), an onomatopoeia for the sound of metal objects clanging together, such as keys or coins dropping.

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 诜 as relating to spoken words.
先 (xiān) has diverged substantially in sound from shēn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: "诜"是一个非常罕见的古字。
example.pinyin: "Shēn" shì yī gè fēicháng hǎnjiàn de gǔzì.
example.english: "Shen" is a very rare archaic character.
example.fact: 诜 is one of the rarer characters in modern Chinese, historically appearing in the reduplicated form 诜诜 describing abundance — today it survives mainly in classical texts and the occasional given name.

components.note: 見 (见, to see) marks 視 as relating to looking.
礻 here represents 示 (shì), which gives the sound — an exact match with 視’s reading.

example.hanzi: 他的視力很好。
example.pinyin: Tā de shìlì hěn hǎo.
example.english: His eyesight is very good.
example.fact: 視 is the traditional form of 视 — the semantic component 見/见 ("to see") marks its meaning directly, while the phonetic component 示 (shì) is an exact match for the character’s own reading, a clean example of how phono-semantic compounds work.

meanings: used in 佝僂|佝偻[gou1 lou2]
used in 僂儸|偻㑩[lou2 luo5]

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 偻 as relating to a person’s posture.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 偻’s reading.

example.hanzi: 老人因为骨质疏松而佝偻着背。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén yīnwèi gǔzhì shūsōng ér gōulóu zhe bèi.
example.english: The elderly person is stooped over because of osteoporosis.
example.fact: 偻 appears in 佝偻 (gōulóu), a medical term for a stooped, hunched posture — as in 佝偻病 (gōulóubìng), the Chinese name for rickets, a bone-softening disease historically caused by vitamin D deficiency in children.

etymologyHint: A load that takes great 大 strength 力

components.note: 大 (big) marks the weight or scale of the load.
力 (strength) marks the effort needed to lift or tamp it.

example.hanzi: 工人们用石夯把地面砸实。
example.pinyin: Gōngrénmen yòng shíhāng bǎ dìmiàn zá shí.
example.english: The workers used a stone rammer to pack down the ground.
example.fact: 夯 names both a heavy tool used to compact earth and the action of using it — before modern machinery, teams of workers would chant rhythmically while lifting and dropping a shared stone rammer together, a practice remembered in Chinese folk work-songs (夯歌).

components.note: 门 (gate/door) marks 闱 as relating to an entrance or enclosed space.
韦 (wéi) gives the sound — an exact match with 闱’s reading.

example.hanzi: 科举考试的考场被称为"闱"。
example.pinyin: Kējǔ kǎoshì de kǎochǎng bèi chēngwéi "wéi".
example.english: The examination hall for the imperial exams was called "wei".
example.fact: 闱 named the examination hall for China’s imperial civil service exams (科举), the grueling multi-day tests that for over a thousand years determined who could become a government official — the system was only abolished in 1905.

components.note: 讠 (speech) marks 谖 as relating to spoken words — forgetting, lying.
爰 (yuán) shares the final -uan with xuān, though the initial and tone differ — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 《诗经》中有"永矢弗谖"的誓言。
example.pinyin: 《Shījīng》 zhōng yǒu "yǒng shǐ fú xuān" de shìyán.
example.english: The Book of Songs contains the vow "yong shi fu xuan" (I vow I shall never forget).
example.fact: 谖 is a classical character meaning "to forget", today confined almost entirely to formal or archaic writing — it appears in old vows of remembrance such as "永矢弗谖" ("I swear I shall never forget"), a phrase still occasionally seen inscribed on monuments and gifts.

components.note: 多 (many) marks 夥 as relating to abundance — many, a group.
果 (guǒ) shares the final and tone with huǒ, differing in the initial — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 他们几个人合夥开了一家餐厅。
example.pinyin: Tāmen jǐ gè rén héhuǒ kāile yī jiā cāntīng.
example.english: The few of them partnered up to open a restaurant.
example.fact: 夥 is a variant form of 伙, appearing in the traditional/complex spelling of words like 合夥 ("partnership") still seen in older documents, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, while mainland China standardized on 伙 for everyday use.

meanings: kind of aspen found in Sichuan
used in 枸櫞|枸橼[ju3 yuan2]

components.note: 木 (wood/tree) marks 枸 as a plant.
句 (jù) is close to one of its alternate readings, gōu (as in 高句丽), though it differs from 句’s more common reading jù.

example.hanzi: 枸杞是一种常见的养生食材。
example.pinyin: Gǒuqǐ shì yī zhǒng chángjiàn de yǎngshēng shícái.
example.english: Goji berries are a common health-food ingredient.
example.fact: 枸 appears in 枸杞 (gǒuqǐ, "goji berry"), a fruit long used in traditional Chinese medicine and cooking — now also popular worldwide as a "superfood".

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks 膑 as relating to the body — the kneecap.
宾 (bīn) is close to bìn’s reading, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 孙膑是中国古代著名的军事家。
example.pinyin: Sūn Bìn shì Zhōngguó gǔdài zhùmíng de jūnshìjiā.
example.english: Sun Bin was a famous ancient Chinese military strategist.
example.fact: 膑 is part of the name of Sun Bin (孙膑), a legendary military strategist who, according to the Records of the Grand Historian, was cruelly subjected to 膑刑 (kneecap removal) by a jealous rival before going on to win his greatest victories.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 虻 as an insect.
亡 (wáng) has diverged substantially in sound from méng, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 夏天，牛虻经常骚扰牲畜。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān, niúméng jīngcháng sāorǎo shēngchù.
example.english: In summer, horseflies often pester livestock.
example.fact: 虻 names the horsefly, whose bite is notably more painful than a mosquito’s because horseflies use scissor-like mouthparts to cut and lap up blood rather than piercing skin with a needle-like proboscis.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) marks 筠 as relating to bamboo.
均 (jūn) shares the final and tone with yún, though the initial has diverged — a partial match.

example.hanzi: "筠"这个字常用于人名，象征坚韧的品格。
example.pinyin: "Yún" zhège zì cháng yòngyú rénmíng, xiàngzhēng jiānrèn de pǐngé.
example.english: "Yun" is a character often used in given names, symbolizing a resilient character.
example.fact: 筠 poetically refers to the hard outer skin of bamboo, and by extension symbolizes moral integrity — bamboo’s ability to bend without breaking has long made it a metaphor for a principled person who stays flexible under pressure without losing their core values.

etymologyHint: To sweep 帚 away dirt 土

components.note: 土 (earth) marks the dirt being swept away.
帚 (broom) depicts the tool used to sweep.

example.hanzi: 古代治理黄河时常用埽工加固堤坝。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài zhìlǐ Huánghé shí cháng yòng sàogōng jiāgù dībà.
example.english: In ancient times, when managing the Yellow River, "sao" construction was often used to reinforce the dikes.
example.fact: 埽 names a traditional Chinese river-engineering technique, 埽工 (sàogōng), in which bundles of willow branches, reeds, stones, and earth were bound together and sunk into the riverbed to reinforce dikes or plug breaches — used for centuries in managing the flood-prone Yellow River.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) marks 笞 as a bamboo implement — a rod used for beating.
台 (tái) has diverged substantially in sound from chī, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 在古代，笞刑是一种常见的刑罚。
example.pinyin: Zài gǔdài, chīxíng shì yī zhǒng chángjiàn de xíngfá.
example.english: In ancient times, flogging was a common form of punishment.
example.fact: 笞刑 (chīxíng, "flogging with a rod") was one of the "Five Punishments" (五刑) codified in traditional Chinese legal codes for over a thousand years, ranking as a lighter penalty than exile or death.

example.hanzi: 须臾之间，天色骤变。
example.pinyin: Xūyú zhī jiān, tiānsè zhòubiàn.
example.english: In a mere instant, the sky’s color suddenly changed.
example.fact: 臾 exists almost entirely in 须臾 (xūyú), a classical Chinese term for "a brief moment" — used in Buddhist texts translated into Chinese to render fine-grained units of time shorter than an hour.

components.note: 女 (woman) marks 婀 as describing feminine grace.
阿 (ā) shares the level first tone with ē, though the vowel differs — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 她走路的姿态婀娜多姿。
example.pinyin: Tā zǒulù de zītài ēnuó duōzī.
example.english: Her walking posture is graceful and lithe.
example.fact: 婀 exists almost entirely in 婀娜 (ēnuó), a classical term describing graceful, swaying beauty — traditionally used for a woman’s posture or a willow tree bending gently in the wind.

components.note: 王 here represents 玉 (jade) — marking 珞 as a jade/stone ornament.
各 (gè) has diverged substantially in sound from luò, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 佛像上常常佩戴着华丽的璎珞。
example.pinyin: Fóxiàng shàng chángcháng pèidàizhe huálì de yīngluò.
example.english: Buddha statues are often adorned with ornate jeweled necklaces.
example.fact: 珞 appears in 璎珞 (yīngluò), the ornate jeweled necklaces traditionally draped over Buddhist and Bodhisattva statues in Chinese Buddhist art, symbolizing purity and spiritual adornment.

components.note: 米 (rice) marks 粑 as made from rice.
巴 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 粑’s reading.

example.hanzi: 糍粑是中国南方常见的传统小吃。
example.pinyin: Cíbā shì Zhōngguó nánfāng chángjiàn de chuántǒng xiǎochī.
example.english: Ciba (glutinous rice cake) is a common traditional snack in southern China.
example.fact: 糍粑 (cíbā) is a traditional glutinous rice cake made by pounding steamed sticky rice into a smooth, chewy paste — a dish especially associated with southern Chinese and Southeast Asian festival food, similar to Japanese mochi.

components.note: 忄 (heart) marks 怵 as an emotional state — fear.
术 (shù) shares the final and tone with chù, with a related initial — a close match.

example.hanzi: 想起那次事故，他仍心里发怵。
example.pinyin: Xiǎngqǐ nà cì shìgù, tā réng xīnlǐ fāchù.
example.english: Thinking back on that accident, he still feels a chill of fear inside.
example.fact: 怵 appears in the colloquial phrase 心里发怵 (xīnlǐ fāchù, "to feel a twinge of dread inside"), a common Beijing-Mandarin-flavored expression for feeling apprehensive or intimidated.

meanings: used in 繾綣|缱绻[qian3 quan3]

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) contributes a sense of entanglement — attachment, longing.
卷 (juǎn) shares the final and tone with quǎn, with a related initial — a close match.

example.hanzi: 他们对故乡一直缱绻不忘。
example.pinyin: Tāmen duì gùxiāng yīzhí qiǎnquǎn bù wàng.
example.english: They remain deeply attached to their hometown, unable to forget it.
example.fact: 绻 exists almost solely in 缱绻 (qiǎnquǎn), a literary term describing deep emotional attachment or reluctance to part — used for intense romantic longing or nostalgic devotion to one’s homeland alike.

components.note: 歹 (death/bad) marks 殒 as relating to death.
员 (yuán) shares the y- glide with yǔn, though the final and tone differ substantially — a loose match.

example.hanzi: 一颗流星在夜空中殒落。
example.pinyin: Yī kē liúxīng zài yèkōng zhōng yǔnluò.
example.english: A shooting star fell across the night sky.
example.fact: 殒 appears in the literary compounds 殒落 (yǔnluò) and 殒命 (yǔnmìng), formal, poetic ways of saying "to die" or "to perish" — often used metaphorically for a falling star or the death of someone considered great.

components.note: 见 (to see) marks 觊 as relating to gazing at something desired.
岂 (qǐ) has diverged substantially in sound from jì, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 邻国对这片富饶的土地心怀觊觎。
example.pinyin: Línguó duì zhè piàn fùráo de tǔdì xīnhuái jìyú.
example.english: The neighboring country harbors covetous designs on this rich land.
example.fact: 觊 exists only in 觊觎 (jìyú, "to covet") — it and 觎 (rank 4520 in this batch) form one of Chinese’s many "bound" two-character words that essentially never separate, each character being almost meaningless alone.

meanings: name of a mountain in Shandong

components.note: 山 (mountain) marks 崂 as a mountain name.
劳 (láo) gives the sound — an exact match with 崂’s reading.

example.hanzi: 崂山是山东著名的风景区。
example.pinyin: Láoshān shì Shāndōng zhùmíng de fēngjǐngqū.
example.english: Laoshan is a famous scenic area in Shandong.
example.fact: 崂山 (Laoshan), near Qingdao in Shandong, is a sacred site in Taoism and is also known for its natural mineral spring water, long associated with the region’s brewing industry, including the famous Tsingtao Beer founded in Qingdao in 1903.

components.note: 页 (head/page) marks 颧 as relating to the head — the cheekbone.
雚 (guàn) shares the final -uan with quán, though the initial and tone differ — a partial match.

example.hanzi: 他的颧骨很高，轮廓分明。
example.pinyin: Tā de quángǔ hěn gāo, lúnkuò fēnmíng.
example.english: His cheekbones are high, giving his face defined contours.
example.fact: 颧骨 (quángǔ, "cheekbone") is used in both everyday descriptions of facial features and in forensic contexts, where cheekbone structure is one of several skeletal features used to help estimate identity from remains.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 嗑 as an action done with the mouth — cracking seeds with the teeth.
盍 (hé) has diverged substantially in sound from kē, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 看电视的时候，他喜欢嗑瓜子。
example.pinyin: Kàn diànshì de shíhou, tā xǐhuan kē guāzǐ.
example.english: While watching TV, he likes to crack sunflower seeds with his teeth.
example.fact: 嗑瓜子 (kē guāzǐ, "cracking sunflower/watermelon seeds with one’s teeth") is a beloved pastime across China, especially during Lunar New Year gatherings.

components.note: 木 (wood/tree) marks 榛 as a tree.
秦 (qín) has diverged substantially in sound from zhēn, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: 榛子是一种美味的坚果。
example.pinyin: Zhēnzi shì yī zhǒng měiwèi de jiānguǒ.
example.english: Hazelnuts are a delicious nut.
example.fact: 榛子 (zhēnzi, "hazelnut") trees grow wild across northeastern China, and the nut is a key flavoring ingredient in Nutella-style chocolate spreads increasingly popular in the Chinese snack market.

components.note: 日 (sun) marks 昱 as relating to sunlight, brightness.
立 (lì) has diverged substantially in sound from yù, leaving no clear connection in modern Mandarin.

example.hanzi: "昱"这个字常用于人名，寓意光明。
example.pinyin: "Yù" zhège zì cháng yòngyú rénmíng, yùyì guāngmíng.
example.english: The character "yu" is often used in given names, symbolizing brightness.
example.fact: 昱 is used almost exclusively as a personal name character today, chosen for its association with radiant sunlight — it rarely appears in ordinary vocabulary outside of names.

components.note: 虫 (bug) marks 蜴 as a creature classified with reptiles and insects.
易 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜴’s reading.

example.hanzi: 蜥蜴可以在墙壁上快速爬行。
example.pinyin: Xīyì kěyǐ zài qiángbì shàng kuàisù páxíng.
example.english: Lizards can crawl quickly on walls.
example.fact: 蜴 exists only in 蜥蜴 (xīyì, "lizard") — both characters share the same 虫 radical, reflecting how Chinese historically classified many small creeping creatures, including reptiles, under this single category.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) is used broadly for eel-like creatures, including 鳝.
善 (shàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 鳝’s reading.

example.hanzi: 黄鳝是一种营养丰富的食材。
example.pinyin: Huángshàn shì yī zhǒng yíngyǎng fēngfù de shícái.
example.english: The ricefield eel is a nutrient-rich ingredient.
example.fact: 黄鳝 (huángshàn, "ricefield eel") is unusual among fish for breathing air directly through its skin and mouth lining, letting it survive in the shallow, oxygen-poor mud of rice paddies.

meanings: to hold in (usually refers the mouth or eyes)

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 噙 as an action done with the mouth — holding something in it.
禽 (qín) gives the sound — an exact match with 噙’s reading.

example.hanzi: 她噙着眼泪，勉强笑了一下。
example.pinyin: Tā qínzhe yǎnlèi, miǎnqiǎng xiàole yīxià.
example.english: Holding back tears welling in her eyes, she managed a forced smile.
example.fact: 噙 describes eyes "holding" tears that have not yet fallen, as in 噙着眼泪 ("eyes brimming with unshed tears") — a common literary image for suppressed emotion.

components.note: 淼 stacks three 水 ("water") characters to intensify the meaning into "a vast expanse of water".

example.hanzi: "淼"这个字由三个"水"组成，形容水面辽阔无边。
example.pinyin: "Miǎo" zhège zì yóu sān gè "shuǐ" zǔchéng, xíngróng shuǐmiàn liáokuò wúbiān.
example.english: The character "miao" is made up of three "water" characters, describing a vast, boundless expanse of water.
example.fact: 淼 is one of several Chinese characters built by tripling a single component to intensify its meaning — compare 晶 (three 日 "suns," meaning "crystal/sparkling") and 森 (three 木 "trees," meaning "forest").
